A Sensitivity Framework for Assessing External Validity
Ariel Boyarsky∗     Naoki Egami†     Hongseok Namkoong∗
∗Decision, Risk, and Operations Division, Columbia Business School

†Department of Political Science, Statistics and Data Science Center,

Massachusetts Institute of Technology

a.boyarsky@columbia.edu, egami@mit.edu, namkoong@gsb.columbia.edu

Abstract

Assessing the external validity of experimental results is a pervasive challenge in causal inference as internally valid findings need not generalize beyond sites in which the experiments were conducted. Since the number of sites is often smaller than the number of site-level variables that moderate causal effects, we develop a partial identification framework that lets practitioners assess external validity under a wide range of assumptions that allow extrapolation across site-level variables. Our optimization-driven approach can accommodate any affine family of parameter restrictions, such as interaction terms being dominated by direct effects (the “effect hierarchy principle”). Since standard estimating-equation arguments do not apply in our setting—underspecified parameter directions responsible for partial identification make the covariance matrix singular—we develop a novel debiasing approach for estimands given by constrained optimization problems, giving rise to semiparametrically efficient estimators for our flexible partial identification bounds. We illustrate our approach on multi-site microcredit experiments harmonized by Meager [26], whose lending environments differ widely in interest rates, loan sizes, and promotion. Holding out one country at a time, we construct external-validity intervals for the held-out country from the remaining source sites and show how our framework connects different extrapolation assumptions to concrete partial identification bounds.

1 Introduction

Randomized experiments are conducted in particular places and times, under particular implementations. The settings in which their evidence is used rarely match the settings in which it was produced: institutions, program terms, and local economic conditions all change when an intervention moves [8, 13]. When treatment effects vary with these site-level variables, internally valid findings lose external validity outside their source sites [1, 41, 26]. A mature set of methods addresses compositional differences between sites, i.e., differences in characteristics of individuals in each (X-validity in Egami and Hartman [16]’s taxonomy), by holding the conditional treatment effect fixed and adjusting for population compositions [36, 37, 10, 14]. In this paper, our focus is on differences in causal effects inherent to site-level variables (C-validity in Egami and Hartman [16]’s taxonomy).

Consider a policymaker using microcredit experiments in six countries to predict the effect on household revenues in Bosnia and Herzegovina, our main application in Section 6. Interest rates, loan sizes, and promotion differ across countries in the data of Meager [26]. To what extent can the source trials predict the effect in Bosnia when its lending environment differs from those in which the trials were conducted?

We propose a sensitivity framework in which site-level variables directly affect causal effects beyond individual-level variables. The fundamental problem is that there are often fewer source sites than site-level variables to estimate and thus the effects of site-level variables are only partially identified.11 1 This limitation is separate from overlap in individual covariates. Even with the same population composition as the source sites, a target effect can depend on the effects of site-level variables that the source data do not identify. In the example above, there are only six sites but scholars have pointed out more than six site-level variables that can moderate causal effects across sites. In such cases, even if the average treatment effect in each source site were known exactly, the average treatment effect in a new site is often not point-identified.

To address this fundamental identification problem, we consider a partially linear model of the potential outcomes, which we formally introduce in the subsequent sections. For a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}, we have

𝔼P[Y(a)∣X,C]=ga(X)+C⊤βa,\mathbb{E}_{P}[Y(a)\mid X,C]=g_{a}(X)+C^{\top}\beta_{a}, (1.1)

where Y⁡(a)Y(a) is the potential outcome, XX are the unit-level variables, CC are the site-level variables, and 𝔼P\mathbb{E}_{P} denotes the expectation over the source population distribution. gag_{a} is an unrestricted function that captures complex unit-level heterogeneity, and βa∈ℝp\beta_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is a fixed vector of coefficients for site-level variables. Note that unit-level variables XX, such as age and gender, can vary within each site, but site-level variables CC, such as local economic and political conditions, can differ only across sites. Given this model, we can express the average treatment effect in a new target site as ψT=𝔼X∼QT​[g1​(X)−g0​(X)]+cT⊤​(β1−β0)\psi_{T}=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q_{T}}[g_{1}(X)-g_{0}(X)]+c_{T}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}) where QTQ_{T} denotes the target population distribution of XX and cTc_{T} is a vector of site-level variables in the particular target site.

Even though this partially linear model is simple, when the number of sites is smaller than the number of site-level variables CC, as is often the case, the coefficients βa\beta_{a} are typically not identified, which often implies that the average treatment effect in the target site ψT\psi_{T} is also not identified. For partial identification, we retain all coefficient vectors consistent with the source evidence and impose explicit restrictions on their magnitudes, signs, or the size of higher-order terms relative to direct effects of site-level variables (Section 2). Minimizing and maximizing the target effect over these vectors gives partial identification bounds. Varying the restrictions shows how different assumptions affect partial identification bounds. Wide partial identification bounds indicate that substantial uncertainty remains even under the stated restrictions; an unbounded endpoint means that some extrapolations remain unrestricted. An empty feasible set means that the restrictions contradict the source evidence.

The unit-lvel heterogeneity component ga​(X)g_{a}(X) introduces a further challenge because differences in population composition can confound comparisons across sites. We allow outcomes to depend arbitrarily on unit-level covariates XX, provided this dependence remains unchanged across sites within each treatment arm, and adjust for the target distribution of XX. Partialling out XX using the approach of Robinson [32] reduces the source model to a linear system for each arm (Section 3). The resulting matrix is singular when the source sites do not identify all the effects of site-level variables βa\beta_{a}. Errors from regressing site-level variables CC on unit-level covariates XX can nevertheless make the estimated matrix full rank and collapse the feasible set to a point. We develop an estimator that preserves the unidentified coefficient combinations, so regression error cannot create spurious point identification (Section 4).

We develop a debiasing procedure for inference on these partial identification bounds. The theoretical challenge is that each partial identification bound solves a constrained optimization problem whose objective and equality constraints must both be estimated. Estimation error changes the feasible set itself, and because the constraint matrix is singular, arbitrarily small perturbations can make the equalities infeasible. The usual smoothness argument behind debiasing therefore does not apply directly. We overcome this obstacle by proving a first-order expansion for the optimized partial identification bound under our estimator (Section 5). This result establishes that correcting bias in the objective and constraints before optimization removes the first-order effect of nuisance estimation error on the partial identification bounds. Under our regularity conditions, we obtain valid confidence intervals while allowing flexible estimation of unit-level heterogeneity.

We use the microcredit experiments to examine how modeling choices affect conclusions about a new lending environment (Section 6). Comparing alternative restrictions shows which assumptions are needed to determine the sign or magnitude of the target effect. The same restriction can substantially narrow the partial identification bounds for one target while leaving another largely unresolved, depending on the contexts represented in the source experiments. Varying the target’s lending terms and removing source sites then distinguishes sensitivity to the target setting from dependence on particular source experiments.

Related work.

Methods for generalizing experiments identify target effects by adjusting for population composition under a stable conditional treatment response and covariate overlap [10, 14, 15, 22], including when several trials supply the source evidence [11]. Our target covariate adjustment uses the same logic, but we also allow site-level variables to change the response. Such heterogeneity is documented in field experiments [1, 26] and corresponds to contextual validity in Egami and Hartman [16]’s taxonomy. We study what source experiments imply when they do not identify all site-level effects needed to predict the target effect. Using these partial identification bounds to choose a treatment requires a further decision criterion, as in work on treatment choice under partial identification and limited external validity [35, 28]. Our analysis characterizes the range of target effects under stated restrictions; a policy decision also requires a welfare criterion and a stance toward ambiguity.

Sensitivity analyses for external validity relax transportability assumptions by allowing omitted effect modifiers [30, 20] or explicit deviations from exchangeability across study participation [12]. Other approaches assess external validity by imposing covariate-balancing constraints under unmeasured effect modification [31], restricting differences between source and target outcome distributions [2], allowing for the violation of the overlap assumption [19], or evaluating worst-case treatment effects over subpopulations [21]. We vary coefficients governing how site context changes treated and control outcomes, while allowing heterogeneous individual-level treatment effects that remain unchanged across sites. Following the partial-identification approach of Manski [25], we retain every coefficient vector consistent with the source evidence and the stated restrictions. Multiple experiments constrain these coefficients, and restrictions on their signs and magnitudes limit the remaining target extrapolations. Our sensitivity analysis describes the underidentification that remains under the additive response model; it does not assess violations of that model.

2 Extrapolation with a small number of sites

We begin with a warm-up in which there is no unit-level covariate XX and the source-site mean outcomes are known. This separates the modeling and identification questions from sampling uncertainty. Our framework then reduces to a regression across sites, with potentially more coefficients than the source experiments can identify. We first formulate the target partial identification bounds, then describe how the analyst’s choice of site-level variables and parameter restrictions determines what can be learned. A two-site example illustrates how these choices affect the partial identification bounds. We introduce the unit-level variable XX in Section 3 and address estimation from finite samples in Section 4.

2.1 A partial-identification framework

In the microcredit example, we observe experiments in a small number of countries whose lending environments differ in interest rates, loan sizes, and promotion. Let cs∈ℝpc_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} describe the site-level variables of source site s=1,…,Ss=1,\ldots,S, and let cT∈ℝpc_{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} describe the target site. The source site-level vector CC takes one of the values c1,…,cSc_{1},\ldots,c_{S}. We choose this site-level basis before the analysis; it may include raw characteristics, their squares, and their interactions. Without a unit-level covariate XX, randomization and consistency identify each source potential-outcome mean ma,s=𝔼⁡[Y⁡(a)∣C=cs]m_{a,s}=\mathbb{E}[Y(a)\mid C=c_{s}], where Y⁡(a)Y(a) is the outcome under treatment arm a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}.

We assume that site-level variables enter each potential-outcome mean linearly,

ma,s=αa+cs⊤βa,a∈{0,1},s=1,…,S,m_{a,s}=\alpha_{a}+c_{s}^{\top}\beta_{a},\qquad a\in\{0,1\},\quad s=1,\ldots,S, (2.1)

and that the same intercepts and coefficients govern the target means. Subtracting the mean at source site 1 removes the intercept and gives

(cs−c1)⊤βa=ma,s−ma,1,s=2,…,S,a∈{0,1}.(c_{s}-c_{1})^{\top}\beta_{a}=m_{a,s}-m_{a,1},\qquad s=2,\ldots,S,\quad a\in\{0,1\}. (2.2)

These are S−1S-1 linear equations for each vector of pp coefficients. If p>S−1p>S-1, some coefficient combinations remain unidentified even when every source mean is known. In the microcredit analysis for Bosnia, six source sites supply at most five independent comparisons for nine site-level terms. At least four linear combinations of each site-level vector are therefore undetermined. Additional observations within each source site improve the precision of each source mean, but cannot supply another comparison across site-level variables.

Under (2.1), the target average treatment effect is

ψT=m1,1−m0,1+(cT−c1)⊤​(β1−β0).\psi_{T}=m_{1,1}-m_{0,1}+(c_{T}-c_{1})^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}). (2.3)

The source sites identify this effect if cT−c1c_{T}-c_{1} is a linear combination of the site-level differences {cs−c1:s=2,…,S}\{c_{s}-c_{1}:s=2,\ldots,S\}. Otherwise, coefficients that fit the same source means can imply different target effects. We limit these extrapolations by imposing substantive restrictions on the coefficients.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} contain the coefficient vectors β=(β0⊤,β1⊤)⊤\beta=(\beta_{0}^{\top},\beta_{1}^{\top})^{\top} allowed by the analyst’s restrictions. The vectors consistent with both the restrictions and the source means form the feasible set

ℱ(0)={β∈ℛ:(cs−c1)⊤βa=ma,s−ma,1,s=2,…,S,a∈{0,1}}.\mathcal{F}^{(0)}=\left\{\beta\in\mathcal{R}:(c_{s}-c_{1})^{\top}\beta_{a}=m_{a,s}-m_{a,1},\;s=2,\ldots,S,\;a\in\{0,1\}\right\}. (2.4)

The extreme target effects over this set are the partial identification bounds,

v−(0)=m1,1−m0,1+infβ∈ℱ(0)(cT−c1)⊤​(β1−β0),v+(0)=m1,1−m0,1+supβ∈ℱ(0)(cT−c1)⊤​(β1−β0).\begin{split}v_{-}^{(0)}&=m_{1,1}-m_{0,1}+\inf_{\beta\in\mathcal{F}^{(0)}}(c_{T}-c_{1})^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}),\\ v_{+}^{(0)}&=m_{1,1}-m_{0,1}+\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal{F}^{(0)}}(c_{T}-c_{1})^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}).\end{split} (2.5)

The optimizing coefficients give the extreme target effects allowed by the data and restrictions. Relaxing a restriction can only widen the partial identification bounds. Tightening it narrows the range of possible effects, but may eventually exclude every coefficient vector consistent with the source evidence.

2.2 Choosing parameter restrictions

The site-level basis determines which features of the site environment can change outcomes. Parameter restrictions determine how much those features can matter. Their interpretation depends on the scale of the site-level variables, which we fix before choosing the restrictions.

Example 1: Magnitude caps.

A magnitude cap imposes |βa,j|≤Mj|\beta_{a,j}|\leq M_{j} for chosen constants MjM_{j}. In the microcredit application, we scale each site-level variable by its standard deviation across source sites. The cap then limits the revenue change attributed to a one-standard-deviation change in that term, holding the others fixed. We set the cap to one standard deviation of the outcome and can vary it to examine how the target partial identification bounds depend on the allowed effect sizes.

Example 2: Effect hierarchy principle.

The effect hierarchy principle from the design of experiments, also called effect ordering or hierarchical ordering, states that lower-order terms are more likely to matter than higher-order terms [18, 27]. It is widely used in statistics, for example in hierarchical interaction models [5, 24]. We use a stronger restriction that compares the magnitude of every higher-order coefficient with every direct coefficient. Write C=(CD⊤,CH⊤)⊤C=(C_{D}^{\top},C_{H}^{\top})^{\top} for the pDp_{D} direct terms and pHp_{H} higher-order terms, and partition each βa\beta_{a} accordingly. For a sensitivity level κ≥0\kappa\geq 0,

|βa,H,j|≤κ​|βa,D,k|for ​a∈{0,1},j=1,…,pH,k=1,…,pD.|\beta_{a,H,j}|\leq\kappa|\beta_{a,D,k}|\quad\text{for }a\in\{0,1\},\ j=1,\ldots,p_{H},\ k=1,\ldots,p_{D}. (2.6)

At κ=0\kappa=0, all higher-order coefficients are zero. At κ=1\kappa=1, each is no larger in magnitude than any direct coefficient in the same treatment arm. Larger values relax the comparison. A direct coefficient near zero therefore forces every higher-order coefficient toward zero, so this can be a strong restriction. Varying κ\kappa shows how much the target conclusion depends on it.

Example 3: Aggregate budgets.

An aggregate budget instead limits the sum of higher-order coefficient magnitudes relative to the sum for direct coefficients.

∑j=1pH|βa,H,j|≤κ​∑k=1pD|βa,D,k|,a∈{0,1}.\sum_{j=1}^{p_{H}}|\beta_{a,H,j}|\;\leq\;\kappa\sum_{k=1}^{p_{D}}|\beta_{a,D,k}|,\qquad a\in\{0,1\}. (2.7)

This permits one large higher-order coefficient when the others are small, whereas (2.6) limits each coefficient separately.

Example 4: Sign and shape restrictions.

Subject-matter knowledge can also restrict the sign of particular coefficients. For example, in the microcredit application, a nonpositive direct interest-rate coefficient in the treatment effect gives

β1,APR−β0,APR≤0.\beta_{1,\mathrm{APR}}-\beta_{0,\mathrm{APR}}\leq 0. (2.8)

An analyst could also require effects of site-level variables to increase or decrease across ordered categories, such as discretized interest rates.

We recommend adding restrictions one at a time and reporting how each changes the target partial identification bounds. Varying the sensitivity parameters within each family shows how the conclusion depends on the strength of the restriction. We follow this protocol in Section 6.

2.3 Numerical example

We give a minimal example to provide mathematical intuition for how the source site-level variables, target site-level variables, and parameter restrictions together determine the partial identification bounds. Consider the treatment-effect surface

τ⁡(c)=τ0+c1​θ1+c2​θ2,θj=β1,j−β0,j,j∈{1,2},\tau(c)=\tau_{0}+c_{1}\theta_{1}+c_{2}\theta_{2},\qquad\theta_{j}=\beta_{1,j}-\beta_{0,j},\quad j\in\{1,2\}, (2.9)

where jj indexes the two site-level variables, and c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} are the coordinates of the site-level vector in this example. Source sites (0,0)(0,0) and (1,1)(1,1) identify τ0\tau_{0} and the sum ρ=θ1+θ2\rho=\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}. Every coefficient pair on the blue line in Figure 1 therefore fits both source effects. At target site (2,2)(2,2), the effect is τ0+2​ρ\tau_{0}+2\rho and is point identified. At target site (1,0)(1,0), the effect is τ0+θ1\tau_{0}+\theta_{1}, which varies along the blue line. The same source evidence can therefore identify the effect at one target and leave it undetermined at another.

Impose a magnitude cap |θj|≤M|\theta_{j}|\leq M directly on the treatment-effect coefficients. This leaves the orange segment and restricts the effect at (1,0)(1,0) by

[τ0+max⁡{−M,ρ−M},τ0+min⁡{M,ρ+M}],|ρ|≤2​M.\left[\tau_{0}+\max\{-M,\rho-M\},\;\tau_{0}+\min\{M,\rho+M\}\right],\qquad|\rho|\leq 2M. (2.10)

For ρ=1.2\rho=1.2 and M=1M=1, as shown in Figure 1, the partial identification bounds are [τ0+0.2,τ0+1][\tau_{0}+0.2,\,\tau_{0}+1]. The interval tightens as MM falls. If |ρ|>2​M|\rho|>2M, no coefficient pair satisfies both the cap and the source evidence.

3 A partial-identification framework with unit-level covariates

We now introduce unit-level covariates XX. The model in Section 2 allowed site-level variables to explain differences in source means. Here we separate site-level effects from differences in population composition by allowing an unrestricted response to XX in each treatment arm. Partialling out these responses gives a linear system analogous to (2.2). We characterize which target effects this system identifies and combine it with the parameter restrictions from Section 2.2.

We denote our observations O=(Y,A,X,C)O=(Y,A,X,C), where A∈{0,1}A\in\{0,1\} is treatment, XX contains unit-level covariates, and C∈ℝpC\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is the site-level vector shared by every observation in the same site. We choose the basis of CC before the analysis; it may contain raw site characteristics and their transformations. The source distribution PP pools the SS sites, and within each site, we assume treatment is randomized with known probability ea​(x,c)=ℙP​(A=a∣X=x,C=c)e_{a}(x,c)=\mathbb{P}_{P}(A=a\mid X=x,C=c), bounded away from zero. The target is described by a site-level profile cT∈ℝpc_{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and a distribution X∼QTX\sim Q_{T} of unit-level covariates, from which a sample is available. This sample can come from a census, survey, or even a prior over the unit-level covariates. Treatment and outcome data come only from the source (observed) sites.22 2 The pair (QT,cT)(Q_{T},c_{T}) can be read as a conditional of one extended population: adjoin a target site to the SS source sites and define the covariate law at that site to be QTQ_{T} with target site-level variable cTc_{T}, leaving the source conditionals P(X∈⋅∣C=cs)P(X\in\cdot\mid C=c_{s}) unchanged. Every target-subscripted object is then a conditional of this single law at the target site. We keep the explicit pair for two reasons. First, the conditioning must be on a site label rather than on the site-level value: P(⋅∣C=cT)P(\,\cdot\mid C=c_{T}) is undefined when cTc_{T} lies outside the source support, and when cTc_{T} coincides with an observed profile it describes units already in the source sites, whose effect is point identified (A.4), not a new location. Second, the two samples are drawn separately with fixed sizes, and the two-sample notation tracks this in the asymptotic theory.

Randomization lets us express potential-outcome means as regressions of an observable inverse-probability pseudo-outcome. Define

Ra=𝟙{A=a}Yea​(X,C),a∈{0,1}.R_{a}=\frac{\mathbbm{1}\{A=a\}Y}{e_{a}(X,C)},\qquad a\in\{0,1\}. (3.1)

Because treatment is randomized given (X,C)(X,C), the pseudo-outcome satisfies 𝔼P[Ra∣X,C]=𝔼P[Y(a)∣X,C]\mathbb{E}_{P}[R_{a}\mid X,C]=\mathbb{E}_{P}[Y(a)\mid X,C]. This standard transformation does not resolve cross-site extrapolation since 𝔼P[Y(a)∣X=x,C=c]\mathbb{E}_{P}[Y(a)\mid X=x,C=c] may be unidentified for certain values of cc.

3.1 A structured response model

Without a cross-site restriction, the conditional mean at a target site outside the source support can vary arbitrarily without changing the source distribution. We therefore impose an additive structure across sites. Site-level variables enter each potential-outcome surface through linear fixed effects, while heterogeneity in unit-level covariates remains unrestricted.

Assumption A (A Partially Linear Potential Outcome Model with Site-level Effects).

For a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\},

𝔼P[Y(a)∣X,C]=ga(X)+C⊤βa,\mathbb{E}_{P}[Y(a)\mid X,C]=g_{a}(X)+C^{\top}\beta_{a}, (3.2)

where gag_{a} is unrestricted and βa∈ℝp\beta_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is a fixed vector of site-level fixed effects. Treatment is randomized within each source site, consistency holds, and the same functions and coefficients govern the target potential-outcome means at (QT,cT)(Q_{T},c_{T}). We assume QT≪PXQ_{T}\ll P_{X} and write w=d​QT/d​PXw=dQ_{T}/dP_{X}. All second moments below are finite.

With no XX, each gag_{a} is a constant αa\alpha_{a}, recovering (2.1).

In the microcredit application, ga​(X)g_{a}(X) allows revenues under arm aa to vary arbitrarily with household age, education, business ownership, and the other unit-level covariates. The site-level variables CC allow APR, loan size, and promotion to shift each arm’s average outcome by a common amount across households. The model excludes interactions between unit-level covariates and site context. For example, it cannot represent an APR effect that differs with prior business ownership, and adding terms to the basis of CC does not relax this exclusion. Our sensitivity analysis quantifies the underidentification that remains under Assumption A, and cannot assess violations of the additive response structure.

Averaging the response model over the target population gives the target average treatment effect,

ψT=𝔼X∼QT​[g1​(X)−g0​(X)]+cT⊤​(β1−β0).\psi_{T}=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q_{T}}[g_{1}(X)-g_{0}(X)]+c_{T}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}). (3.3)

To express this effect in terms of observable source regressions, take conditional expectations given XX in 𝔼P[Ra∣X,C]=ga(X)+C⊤βa\mathbb{E}_{P}[R_{a}\mid X,C]=g_{a}(X)+C^{\top}\beta_{a}. This gives ga​(x)=𝔼P​[Ra∣X=x]−𝔼P​[C∣X=x]⊤​βag_{a}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{P}[R_{a}\mid X=x]-\mathbb{E}_{P}[C\mid X=x]^{\top}\beta_{a} and therefore

ψT=bT+ℓT⊤​(β1−β0),bT=𝔼X∼QT​[𝔼P​[R1−R0∣X]],ℓT=cT−𝔼X∼QT​[𝔼P​[C∣X]].\psi_{T}=b_{T}+\ell_{T}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}),\qquad\begin{aligned} b_{T}&=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q_{T}}\bigl[\mathbb{E}_{P}[R_{1}-R_{0}\mid X]\bigr],\\ \ell_{T}&=c_{T}-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q_{T}}\bigl[\mathbb{E}_{P}[C\mid X]\bigr].\end{aligned} (3.4)

Equation (3.4) has the same form as (2.3), with the baseline and site-level difference now adjusted for population composition. The term bTb_{T} averages the source regression under the target covariate law and is identified under overlap in XX. The site-level difference ℓT\ell_{T} measures how the target site differs from the source site predicted for target-like units. It multiplies the fixed-effect differences β1−β0\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}, the only unknown quantity in (3.4). Whether ψT\psi_{T} is point identified therefore depends on whether the source sites identify the direction of ℓT\ell_{T}.

3.2 What the source sites identify

Under Assumption A, βa\beta_{a} is the coefficient on CC in a partially linear regression problem. The observable regression

𝔼P[Ra∣X,C]=ga(X)+C⊤βa\mathbb{E}_{P}[R_{a}\mid X,C]=g_{a}(X)+C^{\top}\beta_{a} (3.5)

has RaR_{a} as its outcome, CC as the low-dimensional regressor of interest, and an unrestricted function gag_{a} of the unit-level covariates. Its population minimizers solve

minf,β⁡𝔼P​[{Ra−f⁡(X)−C⊤​β}2].\min_{f,\,\beta}\ \mathbb{E}_{P}\bigl[\{R_{a}-f(X)-C^{\top}\beta\}^{2}\bigr]. (3.6)

Robinson [32] profiles out ff by residualizing both RaR_{a} and CC on XX. The normal equations are

ΣC​βa=𝔼P​[Cov⁡(C,Ra∣X)],a∈{0,1},\Sigma_{C}\,\beta_{a}=\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C,R_{a}\mid X)],\qquad a\in\{0,1\}, (3.7)

where ΣC=𝔼P​[Cov⁡(C∣X)]\Sigma_{C}=\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C\mid X)] measures the variation of site-level variables remaining after adjustment for XX. Since CC takes only SS values, its residuals lie in the span of the S−1S-1 centered site profiles, so rank⁡(ΣC)≤S−1\rankop(\Sigma_{C})\leq S-1. Sampling more units cannot identify the missing directions in site-level variables.

The coefficient vectors consistent with the source conditional means are exactly the solutions

βa=ΣC+​𝔼P​[Cov⁡(C,Ra∣X)]+za,za∈ker⁡(ΣC),\beta_{a}=\Sigma_{C}^{+}\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C,R_{a}\mid X)]+z_{a},\qquad z_{a}\in\kernelop(\Sigma_{C}), (3.8)

where ΣC+\Sigma_{C}^{+} is the Moore–Penrose inverse (Section A.1). Substituting into (3.4) separates the identified component of the target effect from uncertainty along these directions:

ψT=bT+ℓT⊤​ΣC+​𝔼P​[Cov⁡(C,R1−R0∣X)]⏟identified+ℓT⊤​(z1−z0)⏟external-validity uncertainty.\psi_{T}=\underbrace{b_{T}+\ell_{T}^{\top}\Sigma_{C}^{+}\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C,R_{1}-R_{0}\mid X)]}_{\text{identified}}+\underbrace{\ell_{T}^{\top}(z_{1}-z_{0})}_{\text{external-validity uncertainty}}. (3.9)
Corollary 1 (Target point identification).

Assume unrestricted support for the potential outcomes. Without additional restrictions, ψT\psi_{T} is point identified if and only if

ℓT∈range⁡(ΣC),\ell_{T}\in\rangeop(\Sigma_{C}), (3.10)

or, equivalently, ℓT⊤​z=0\ell_{T}^{\top}z=0 for every z∈ker⁡(ΣC)z\in\kernelop(\Sigma_{C}). If the condition fails, the unrestricted target effect is unbounded from above and below. Proof in Appendix A.1.

The span condition (3.10) is not to be confused with overlap over unit-level covariates. A target can have excellent overlap in unit-level covariates and still load on a direction of site-level variables that no source site identifies. Conversely, a target site outside the convex hull of the observed sites can still have a point-identified effect because identification depends on the span of the residualized source profiles, as in the no-XX example of Figure 1. This population singularity also affects estimation. Regressing each coordinate of the site-level variables CC separately on unit-level covariates XX can introduce residual components outside the source-site span, restoring full rank in the sample and erasing the population indeterminacy. Section 4 estimates 𝔼P​[C∣X]\mathbb{E}_{P}[C\mid X] jointly so that the sample program retains the population rank.

3.3 Partial identification bounds after covariate adjustment

We use the same restriction set ℛ\mathcal{R} on β=(β0⊤,β1⊤)⊤\beta=(\beta_{0}^{\top},\beta_{1}^{\top})^{\top} as in Section 2.2. Replacing the no-XX source equations by the residualized normal equations and adjusting the target objective gives

ℱ={β:ΣCβa=𝔼P[Cov(C,Ra∣X)],a∈{0,1},β∈ℛ},\mathcal{F}=\left\{\beta:\ \Sigma_{C}\beta_{a}=\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C,R_{a}\mid X)],\ a\in\{0,1\},\ \beta\in\mathcal{R}\right\}, (3.11)

and we define the sensitivity interval by the extreme target effects

v−=bT+infβ∈ℱℓT⊤​(β1−β0),v+=bT+supβ∈ℱℓT⊤​(β1−β0).\begin{split}v_{-}&=b_{T}+\inf_{\beta\in\mathcal{F}}\ell_{T}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}),\\ v_{+}&=b_{T}+\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal{F}}\ell_{T}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}).\end{split} (3.12)

Every β∈ℱ\beta\in\mathcal{F} reproduces the source conditional means. The two optimization problems project this restricted identified set onto the target effect, and we refer to v−v_{-} and v+v_{+} as the partial identification bounds. If ℱ\mathcal{F} is convex, the partial identification bounds are finite, and the outcome support is unrestricted, every value in [v−,v+][v_{-},v_{+}] is attained by a model consistent with the data and the restriction. The interval is then sharp (Proposition 2). Support restrictions for bounded or binary outcomes can shrink the attainable set. A finite union of polyhedra can instead project to several disjoint intervals. In that case, [v−,v+][v_{-},v_{+}] is their convex hull, and the separate intervals should be retained to display the gaps.

Thus the restrictions retain their interpretation as limits on site-level effects, while adjustment for XX changes both the source constraints and the target objective. With no XX, these programs reduce to (2.5).

4 Estimating partial identification bounds

Each partial identification bound in (3.12) is the value of a constrained optimization problem. We must estimate both the target-effect objective and the linear equations that determine which coefficients fit the source data. Estimating these equations requires care: small errors can make them appear to determine coefficients that the population equations leave unrestricted. The estimated partial identification bounds can then collapse to a point, or the equations can become incompatible with the parameter restrictions. We therefore construct estimates that preserve the linear dependencies implied by the source site-level variables (Section 4.1).

Once this structure is preserved, we address bias in the estimated objective and constraints caused by estimating nuisance functions such as conditional means. Flexible estimates of these functions can converge more slowly than n−1/2n^{-1/2}, so we use standard debiasing corrections to remove the first-order effect of their estimation errors. Unlike the ATE, which is linear in the outcome regressions for a fixed covariate distribution, our partial identification bounds depend nonlinearly on nuisance functions through the objective and constraints of an optimization problem. A natural approach is to solve the optimization problem in each fold and then apply a one-step bias correction. But nuisance error can make even one fold’s constraints infeasible, leaving no estimate to correct. Our approach reverses this order: we debias and pool the inputs, then solve a single optimization problem. Feasibility is therefore required only at the pooled inputs (Section 4.2).

Sampling error also changes which coefficients satisfy the estimated constraints, so standard errors must account for how these changes affect the optimized value. We construct standard errors that remain well defined despite nonunique dual variables (Section 4.3). The simulations in Section 4.4 show why pooling before optimization matters in small samples: it avoids the disagreement across foldwise solutions that can prevent one-step inference.

4.1 Preserving the rank of the equality system

Both sides of the linear equations (3.7) are estimated using residuals from regressing site-level variables CC on unit-level covariates XX. The fitted conditional mean m^C​(x)\widehat{m}_{C}(x) estimates mC​(x)=𝔼P​[C∣X=x]m_{C}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{P}[C\mid X=x] and must respect the linear relationships among the source site-level variables. If we fit the coordinates of mCm_{C} separately, the vector m^C​(Xi)\widehat{m}_{C}(X_{i}) need not remain in the affine span of the source-site profiles. The residuals Ci−m^C​(Xi)C_{i}-\widehat{m}_{C}(X_{i}) can then acquire components in directions of site-level variables that do not vary across the observed sites. Even small components in these directions can make 𝔼^​[Cov^​(C∣X)]\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{{\rm Cov}}(C\mid X)] full rank. The plug-in equalities may consequently replace an affine population feasible set with a single coefficient vector. If that vector violates the restrictions in ℛ\mathcal{R}, the sample program becomes infeasible. Regression error can therefore create spurious point identification or infeasibility. Keeping the fitted residuals in the source-site span prevents these errors.

The finite set of source site-level variables gives a simple way to preserve rank. Since CC takes one of the values c1,…,cSc_{1},\ldots,c_{S}, its conditional mean mC​(X)m_{C}(X) is a weighted average of these same site profiles. Subtracting the conditional mean therefore removes their common location and leaves a vector in

𝒱C=span{cs−c1:s=2,…,S},\mathcal{V}_{C}=\operatorname{span}\{c_{s}-c_{1}:s=2,\ldots,S\}, (4.1)

so C−mC​(X)∈𝒱CC-m_{C}(X)\in\mathcal{V}_{C}. It follows that range⁡(ΣC)⊆𝒱C\rangeop(\Sigma_{C})\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{C} and 𝔼P​[Cov⁡(C,Ra∣X)]∈𝒱C\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C,R_{a}\mid X)]\in\mathcal{V}_{C}. The population equality system thus varies only along the directions of site-level variables present in the source sites.

We impose the same restriction on the fitted residuals. We estimate the full vector of site probabilities ps​(x)=ℙ⁡(C=cs∣X=x)p_{s}(x)=\mathbb{P}(C=c_{s}\mid X=x) with a joint classifier and set

m^C​(x)=∑s=1Scs​p^s​(x).\widehat{m}_{C}(x)=\sum_{s=1}^{S}c_{s}\widehat{p}_{s}(x). (4.2)

The fitted probabilities sum to one, so both CiC_{i} and m^C​(Xi)\widehat{m}_{C}(X_{i}) are affine combinations of the source profiles. Their difference lies in 𝒱C\mathcal{V}_{C} exactly, regardless of the classifier’s estimation error. We use this same residual in every estimated moment involving CC. Estimation error can then move these moments within 𝒱C\mathcal{V}_{C}, but it cannot introduce a direction orthogonal to the observed site variation.

To remove the redundant equations, let r=dim(𝒱C)r=\dim(\mathcal{V}_{C}) and let BC∈ℝp×rB_{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times r} have orthonormal columns spanning 𝒱C\mathcal{V}_{C}. The sample moments can be written as

𝔼^​[Cov^​(C∣X)]=BC​Ω^​BC⊤,𝔼^​[Cov^​(C,Ra∣X)]=BC​ς^a,\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{{\rm Cov}}(C\mid X)]=B_{C}\widehat{\Omega}B_{C}^{\top},\qquad\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{{\rm Cov}}(C,R_{a}\mid X)]=B_{C}\widehat{\varsigma}_{a},

where Ω^=BC⊤​𝔼^​[Cov^​(C∣X)]​BC\widehat{\Omega}=B_{C}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{{\rm Cov}}(C\mid X)]B_{C} and ς^a=BC⊤​𝔼^​[Cov^​(C,Ra∣X)]\widehat{\varsigma}_{a}=B_{C}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{{\rm Cov}}(C,R_{a}\mid X)]. We give the solver the reduced equalities

Ω^​BC⊤​βa=ς^a,a∈{0,1}.\widehat{\Omega}B_{C}^{\top}\beta_{a}=\widehat{\varsigma}_{a},\qquad a\in\{0,1\}.

Under the within-span eigenvalue condition in Assumption C, Ω^\widehat{\Omega} is invertible with probability approaching one. On this event, the right-hand side is in the range of 𝔼^​[Cov^​(C∣X)]\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{{\rm Cov}}(C\mid X)], and the reduced system has full row rank. The reduced equalities remove only the redundant rows of the sample analogue of (3.7). They therefore define the same feasible coefficient vectors and the same partial identification bound while preserving the population rank.

4.2 Debiasing the inputs before optimization

Preserving rank does not ensure that each fold’s estimated source equations are compatible with the parameter restrictions. The natural one-step approach, which optimizes in each fold before correcting nuisance bias, can therefore fail before the correction is even defined.

We avoid this requirement by correcting the objective and source moments directly using regression residuals. We then pool the corrected inputs across folds and optimize once, so only the pooled optimization problem must be feasible. The construction below first gives the corrections for the source and target inputs, then combines them into the estimator. The optimizer and dual variables enter only the standard error, for which our theory requires consistency (Section 5). We give the one-step benchmark in Section D.2 and examine the practical consequences of optimizing before pooling in Section 4.4.

Write v⁡(Γ)v(\Gamma) for the lower partial identification bound in (3.12), where

Γ=(bT,ℓT,ΣC,𝔼P​[Cov⁡(C,R0∣X)],𝔼P​[Cov⁡(C,R1∣X)]).\Gamma=(b_{T},\ell_{T},\Sigma_{C},\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C,R_{0}\mid X)],\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C,R_{1}\mid X)]). (4.3)

The upper partial identification bound uses the corresponding maximization. For a finite union of polyhedra, we optimize over each polyhedron and take the outer extrema. Our scores use the joint and marginal outcome regressions

μa(x,c)=𝔼P[Y∣A=a,X=x,C=c],μa(x)=𝔼P[Ra∣X=x],\mu_{a}(x,c)=\mathbb{E}_{P}[Y\mid A=a,X=x,C=c],\qquad\mu_{a}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{P}[R_{a}\mid X=x], (4.4)

along with mCm_{C}. We estimate the inputs with orthogonal scores, whose expectations are insensitive to first-order nuisance error, and evaluate each score on observations held out from fitting [4, 29, 38, 9].

Debiased program inputs.

Randomized treatment assignment makes the pseudo-outcome RaR_{a} noisy. We use the standard augmented outcome based on the joint outcome regression μa​(X,C)\mu_{a}(X,C):

Ua=μa​(X,C)+𝟙{A=a}ea​(X,C)​{Y−μa​(X,C)}.U_{a}=\mu_{a}(X,C)+\frac{\mathbbm{1}\{A=a\}}{e_{a}(X,C)}\{Y-\mu_{a}(X,C)\}. (4.5)

Both RaR_{a} and UaU_{a} have conditional mean μa​(X,C)\mu_{a}(X,C), so they define the same population moments. We use UaU_{a} to reduce variation from randomized treatment assignment. The treatment probabilities are known from the randomized design.

Let O1,…,On∼iidPO_{1},\ldots,O_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm iid}}{{\sim}}P be the source observations and let XT,1,…,XT,nT∼iidQTX_{T,1},\ldots,X_{T,n_{T}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm iid}}{{\sim}}Q_{T} be an independent covariate sample from the target. We fit the joint and marginal outcome regressions separately. Suppressing fold indices, the source moments are

U^a,i=μ^a​(Xi,Ci)+𝟙{Ai=a}ea​(Xi,Ci)​{Yi−μ^a​(Xi,Ci)},𝔼^​[Cov^​(C∣X)]=1n​∑i=1n{Ci−m^C​(Xi)}​{Ci−m^C​(Xi)}⊤,𝔼^​[Cov^​(C,Ra∣X)]=1n∑i=1n{Ci−m^C(Xi)}{U^a,i−μ^a(Xi)},a∈{0,1}.\begin{split}\widehat{U}_{a,i}&=\widehat{\mu}_{a}(X_{i},C_{i})+\frac{\mathbbm{1}\{A_{i}=a\}}{e_{a}(X_{i},C_{i})}\{Y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{a}(X_{i},C_{i})\},\\ \widehat{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{{\rm Cov}}(C\mid X)]&=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{C_{i}-\widehat{m}_{C}(X_{i})\}\{C_{i}-\widehat{m}_{C}(X_{i})\}^{\top},\\ \widehat{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{{\rm Cov}}(C,R_{a}\mid X)]&=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{C_{i}-\widehat{m}_{C}(X_{i})\}\{\widehat{U}_{a,i}-\widehat{\mu}_{a}(X_{i})\},\qquad a\in\{0,1\}.\end{split} (4.6)

Iterated expectations set the first-order derivatives with respect to mCm_{C} and the marginal μa\mu_{a} to zero. Randomization sets the derivative with respect to the joint μa\mu_{a} to zero because 𝔼[𝟙{A=a}/ea(X,C)∣X,C]=1\mathbb{E}[\mathbbm{1}\{A=a\}/e_{a}(X,C)\mid X,C]=1.

The target inputs average regressions under QTQ_{T}, but their residual corrections use source observations. We reweight those residuals using the density ratio

w​(x)=d​QTd​PX​(x).w(x)=\frac{dQ_{T}}{dP_{X}}(x). (4.7)

Each augmented transport score combines a target-sample regression average with a reweighted source-sample residual correction:

b^T=1nT​∑i=1nT{μ^1​(XT,i)−μ^0​(XT,i)}+1n∑i=1nw^(Xi)[{U^1,i−μ^1(Xi)}−{U^0,i−μ^0(Xi)}],ℓ^T=cT−1nT​∑i=1nTm^C​(XT,i)−1n​∑i=1nw^​(Xi)​{Ci−m^C​(Xi)}.\begin{split}\widehat{b}_{T}&=\frac{1}{n_{T}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{T}}\{\widehat{\mu}_{1}(X_{T,i})-\widehat{\mu}_{0}(X_{T,i})\}\\ &\quad+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{w}(X_{i})\big[\{\widehat{U}_{1,i}-\widehat{\mu}_{1}(X_{i})\}-\{\widehat{U}_{0,i}-\widehat{\mu}_{0}(X_{i})\}\big],\\ \widehat{\ell}_{T}&=c_{T}-\frac{1}{n_{T}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{T}}\widehat{m}_{C}(X_{T,i})-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{w}(X_{i})\{C_{i}-\widehat{m}_{C}(X_{i})\}.\end{split} (4.8)

The density-ratio error enters the bias only through its product with regression error. Together with the source scores, this leaves a remainder that is op(n−1/2)o_{p}(n^{-1/2}) under the product-rate conditions in Assumption D.33 3 If the target law QTQ_{T} is known exactly, say from a census, we replace each empirical target average in (4.8) by the exact QTQ_{T} integral of the fitted regression. The source corrections are unchanged, and no target sampling uncertainty enters the theory.

Identification requires QT≪PXQ_{T}\ll P_{X}; inference also requires the density-ratio moment conditions in Section 5. Neither condition requires the target site cTc_{T} to lie in the source support.

Pooling the corrected inputs.

Collect the nuisance functions as

η=(mC,μ0,μ1,w),\eta=(m_{C},\mu_{0},\mu_{1},w), (4.9)

where each outcome regression enters through its joint and marginal forms. We split the source and target samples into paired folds, fit the nuisance functions outside each fold, and evaluate (4.6) and (4.8) on its held-out observations. Pooling these scores by observation gives Γ^\widehat{\Gamma}. We substitute these inputs into (3.12), so the estimator of the lower partial identification bound is

v^−pd=v⁡(Γ^).\widehat{v}^{\textsc{pd}}_{-}=v(\widehat{\Gamma}). (4.10)

We retain the optimizer and dual variables for the standard error. The point estimate requires no further correction. Algorithm 1 summarizes the estimator.

4.3 Standard errors

Sampling error changes both the target-effect objective and the set of coefficients satisfying the source constraints. Standard errors must therefore account for how an estimated constraint shifts the optimal value, even after we have removed first-order nuisance bias from the inputs. The optimizer measures sensitivity to the objective, while the equality dual variables measure sensitivity to the constraints.

This creates an apparent ambiguity: the redundant source equations admit multiple dual solutions. We resolve it using the same reduced equality system that preserves rank. All admissible perturbations of the source equations lie in 𝒱C\mathcal{V}_{C}, so only a dual variable’s projection onto this span can affect the partial identification bound. The dual λ¯a\bar{\lambda}_{a} from the reduced system in Section 4.1 gives the representative

λa=BC​λ¯a.\lambda_{a}=B_{C}\bar{\lambda}_{a}. (4.11)

This is the minimum-norm full dual and has a unique population target under our regularity conditions. Thus the standard error does not depend on an arbitrary choice among full dual solutions.

Let β∗=(β0∗,β1∗)\beta^{*}=(\beta_{0}^{*},\beta_{1}^{*}) be the population optimizer for the lower partial identification bound. An envelope argument combines the objective and constraint sensitivities to give

v^−v=(b^T−bT)+(ℓ^T−ℓT)⊤​(β1∗−β0∗)+∑a∈{0,1}λa⊤{(𝔼^[Cov^(C,Ra∣X)]−𝔼P[Cov(C,Ra∣X)])−(𝔼^[Cov^(C∣X)]−ΣC)β∗a}+op(n−1/2).\begin{gathered}\widehat{v}-v=(\widehat{b}_{T}-b_{T})+(\widehat{\ell}_{T}-\ell_{T})^{\top}(\beta^{*}_{1}-\beta^{*}_{0})\\ +\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}}\lambda_{a}^{\top}\bigl\{(\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{{\rm Cov}}(C,R_{a}\mid X)]-\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C,R_{a}\mid X)])-(\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{{\rm Cov}}(C\mid X)]-\Sigma_{C})\beta^{*}_{a}\bigr\}+o_{p}(n^{-1/2}).\end{gathered} (4.12)

Substituting the input scores gives the source influence function

ϕ⁡(O)=w⁡(X)​[{U1−μ1​(X)}−{U0−μ0​(X)}+(β1∗−β0∗)⊤​{mC​(X)−C}]+λ0⊤​(C−mC​(X))​{U0−μ0​(X)−(C−mC​(X))⊤​β0∗}+λ1⊤​(C−mC​(X))​{U1−μ1​(X)−(C−mC​(X))⊤​β1∗},\begin{split}\phi(O)&=w(X)\Big[\{U_{1}-\mu_{1}(X)\}-\{U_{0}-\mu_{0}(X)\}+(\beta^{*}_{1}-\beta^{*}_{0})^{\top}\{m_{C}(X)-C\}\Big]\\ &\quad+\lambda_{0}^{\top}(C-m_{C}(X))\bigl\{U_{0}-\mu_{0}(X)-(C-m_{C}(X))^{\top}\beta^{*}_{0}\bigr\}\\ &\quad+\lambda_{1}^{\top}(C-m_{C}(X))\bigl\{U_{1}-\mu_{1}(X)-(C-m_{C}(X))^{\top}\beta^{*}_{1}\bigr\},\end{split} (4.13)

and, when the target covariates are sampled,

ϕT​(XT)=μ1​(XT)−μ0​(XT)+{cT−mC​(XT)}⊤​(β1∗−β0∗)−v.\phi_{T}(X_{T})=\mu_{1}(X_{T})-\mu_{0}(X_{T})+\{c_{T}-m_{C}(X_{T})\}^{\top}(\beta^{*}_{1}-\beta^{*}_{0})-v. (4.14)

Both functions have mean zero. The first line of (4.13) accounts for estimation of the target inputs, and the remaining lines account for the source constraints. Equation (4.14) captures sampling variation in the target covariate distribution.

For the upper partial identification bound, we use its own optimizer and dual; a dual obtained by minimizing the negative objective must be multiplied by −1-1. Section 5 establishes the expansion and consistency of these optimization estimates on the domain of moments generated by the observed sites.

We evaluate the influence functions at the cross-fitted nuisances and each partial identification bound’s optimizer and dual. If σ^j2\widehat{\sigma}_{j}^{2} and σ^T,j2\widehat{\sigma}_{T,j}^{2} are their empirical source and target variances, the standard error for endpoint j∈{−,+}j\in\{-,+\} is se^j=(σ^j2/n+σ^T,j2/nT)1/2\widehat{\mathrm{se}}_{j}=(\widehat{\sigma}_{j}^{2}/n+\widehat{\sigma}_{T,j}^{2}/n_{T})^{1/2}. Its pointwise Wald interval is v^j±z1−α/2​se^j\widehat{v}_{j}\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat{\mathrm{se}}_{j}. When QTQ_{T} is known and integrated exactly, we omit the target variance term.

4.4 Numerical evidence for pooling before optimization

We study a finite-sample obstacle to the one-step correction: sign mismatch across folds. Under effect hierarchy (2.6), each sign pattern of the direct coefficients defines a linear program. A sign mismatch occurs when the folds select different optimizing sign patterns for either the lower or upper partial identification bound. The standard one-step correction (Algorithm 2) requires agreement across folds and withholds an interval when this condition fails, even if every fold’s optimization problem is feasible. Our estimator (Algorithm 1) pools the corrected inputs before optimizing, so it eliminates this source of failure. At n=500n=500, sign mismatch prevents one-step inference in 89 percent of replications, while our approach permits inference in every replication. We examine how this mismatch and interval coverage change with sample size.

We focus on the design most likely to expose this problem: partial identification with nonlinear nuisance functions. Outcomes follow Y=gA​(X)+C⊤​βA+εY=g_{A}(X)+C^{\top}\beta_{A}+\varepsilon, where ε∼N⁡(0,1)\varepsilon\sim N(0,1), and treatment probabilities vary across sites from 0.350.35 to 0.650.65. The unit-level covariates include a binary, a binomial, and a Gaussian variable. Their relationships with site and outcome are nonlinear, and we estimate the nuisance functions with gradient-boosted trees. Each source sample of size nn is paired with an independent target covariate sample of the same size. Four sites span only three of six site-level terms, so three directions remain unidentified. We obtain finite partial identification bounds by imposing the box |βa,j|≤2.5|\beta_{a,j}|\leq 2.5 and effect hierarchy (2.6) at κ=1\kappa=1, which requires each higher-order site-level coefficient to be no larger in absolute value than every direct site-level coefficient in the same treatment arm. Conditioning on the signs of the three direct coefficients in each arm gives 64 linear programs. We compare against the benchmark using the same data draw, outer folds, nuisance learner class, restrictions, and solver. We use 100 replications at each n∈{500,1,000,2,500,5,000,10,000}n\in\{500,1{,}000,2{,}500,5{,}000,10{,}000\}.

Panel (a) of Figure 2 shows that the probability of sign mismatch for the standard one-step correction is 0.89 at n=500n=500, 0.45 at n=1,000n=1{,}000, and 0.11 at n=2,500n=2{,}500; no mismatch occurs from n=5,000n=5{,}000 onward. Every fold-level optimization problem is feasible, so the failures arise entirely from sign mismatch. Panel (b) shows poor conditional coverage for the standard one-step correction in the two smallest samples, based on the 11 and 55 replications without sign mismatch. From n=5,000n=5{,}000 onward, both algorithms permit inference in every replication and their coverage is similar. These results favor our estimator because pooling before optimization eliminates sign mismatch across folds. The demonstrated advantage concerns whether inference is possible in small samples; coverage is similar once the folds agree, and this design does not compare the methods under a single polyhedron.

5 Asymptotic theory

We develop debiased inference for partial identification bounds defined by optimization problems with estimated equality constraints. Estimation changes both the objective and which coefficients satisfy the source equations. Even with the objective held fixed, errors in the constraints shift the feasible set and hence the optimized value. The equality dual variables measure this sensitivity, so they must enter the influence function and standard error. Here the equality system is also rank deficient: arbitrary perturbations can destroy feasibility, and redundant equations make the full dual variables nonunique.

To our knowledge, we provide the first debiased Gaussian inference result for partial identification bounds whose rank-deficient equality system has both an estimated coefficient matrix and an estimated right-hand side, allowing nonunique full equality dual variables.44 4 Related results address different constraint structures. Ben-Michael [3] develops debiased inference for conditional linear programs with a known equality-constraint matrix. Kim et al. [23] study inference for optimization solutions with estimated constraints under linear independence of the active constraint gradients. We first establish differentiability along the moment perturbations preserved by our estimator and show that all full dual solutions give the same derivative on this domain. We then prove consistency of the optimizer and reduced dual estimates and combine the derivative with orthogonal scores for both the objective and constraints. This gives valid inference while requiring only consistency of the optimization estimates.

The first step is to control how the estimated equalities change the feasible set. We need to differentiate only along directions in which the estimated moments can vary. An arbitrary perturbation of (3.7) can move 𝔼P​[Cov⁡(C,Ra∣X)]\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C,R_{a}\mid X)] outside range⁡(ΣC)\rangeop(\Sigma_{C}) and make the equality infeasible. Our estimator preserves the source-site span 𝒱C\mathcal{V}_{C}, so we restrict the tangent space to perturbations that preserve this span. Using the basis BCB_{C} from Section 4.1, this domain is

𝒢C={(b,ℓ,BC​Ω​BC⊤,BC​ς0,BC​ς1):(b,ℓ,Ω,ς0,ς1)∈𝒰},\mathcal{G}_{C}=\bigl\{(b,\ell,B_{C}\Omega B_{C}^{\top},B_{C}\varsigma_{0},B_{C}\varsigma_{1}):(b,\ell,\Omega,\varsigma_{0},\varsigma_{1})\in\mathcal{U}\bigr\}, (5.1)

where 𝒰=ℝ×ℝp×𝕊+⁣+r×ℝr×ℝr\mathcal{U}=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{S}_{++}^{r}\times\mathbb{R}^{r}\times\mathbb{R}^{r} is open in the reduced coordinates γ=(b,ℓ,Ω,ς0,ς1)\gamma=(b,\ell,\Omega,\varsigma_{0},\varsigma_{1}). The dual variables translate these changes in the equalities into changes in the optimized value. Their nonuniqueness would leave the influence function ambiguous if different dual solutions assigned different weights to the same estimation error. Restricting the perturbations resolves this problem. Adding a vector in ker⁡(ΣC)\kernelop(\Sigma_{C}) leaves the optimality conditions unchanged, but this component is orthogonal to every admissible perturbation of the source equations. Only the projection of the dual onto 𝒱C\mathcal{V}_{C} affects sensitivity to the constraints. We therefore use λa=BC​λ¯a\lambda_{a}=B_{C}\bar{\lambda}_{a}, where λ¯a\bar{\lambda}_{a} is the reduced equality dual, and establish convergence to this minimum-norm representative.

For one polyhedron, write ℛ={β:G​β≤h}\mathcal{R}=\{\beta:G\beta\leq h\}. The following assumption ensures that the perturbed equalities remain compatible with these restrictions locally and that the optimizing coefficients remain bounded. It also supplies a relative interior point. Uniqueness is required for the population optimizer and the reduced dual, so perturbations select a single linear derivative. Without this uniqueness, the partial identification bound can have only directional derivatives, and Gaussian inference need not apply.

Assumption B (Regular partial identification bound).

For each partial identification bound and its population-optimal polyhedron: (i) throughout a neighborhood 𝒰0⊂𝒰\mathcal{U}_{0}\subset\mathcal{U} of the population reduced input γ∗\gamma^{*}, the program is feasible, its optimal value is attained and finite, and is locally bounded as a function of the moments; (ii) at γ∗\gamma^{*}, relative Slater holds after redundant equality rows are removed and after deleting only inequalities that are implied by the reduced equalities throughout 𝒰0\mathcal{U}_{0}; (iii) the population lower level set through a Slater point is bounded after orienting the partial identification bound as a minimization; and (iv) the population optimizer and the reduced KKT dual pair are unique at γ∗\gamma^{*}. The restriction matrices (G,h)(G,h) are held fixed along every moment perturbation.

Under Assumption B, the partial identification bound vv is Hadamard differentiable on 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C} tangentially to its tangent space. For an admissible perturbation Γ˙=(b˙,ℓ˙,Σ˙,d˙0,d˙1)\dot{\Gamma}=(\dot{b},\dot{\ell},\dot{\Sigma},\dot{d}_{0},\dot{d}_{1}),

D​v​(Γ)​[Γ˙]=b˙+ℓ˙⊤​(β1∗−β0∗)+∑a∈{0,1}λa⊤​(d˙a−Σ˙​βa∗),Dv(\Gamma)[\dot{\Gamma}]=\dot{b}+\dot{\ell}^{\top}(\beta^{*}_{1}-\beta^{*}_{0})+\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}}\lambda_{a}^{\top}(\dot{d}_{a}-\dot{\Sigma}\beta^{*}_{a}), (5.2)

where β∗\beta^{*} is the population optimizer. The first two terms capture error in the objective. The residual d˙a−Σ˙​βa∗\dot{d}_{a}-\dot{\Sigma}\beta_{a}^{*} measures how the perturbed equality fails at the population optimizer, and its dual weight gives the resulting first-order change in the partial identification bound. Thus the derivative accounts for estimation error on both sides of the equality. Since this residual lies in 𝒱C\mathcal{V}_{C}, every full dual representative gives the same derivative. Lemma 3 proves this formula, allowing us to apply the tangential delta method [39, Theorem 20.8] despite the singular equality system.

The same regularity conditions ensure consistency of the optimizer and reduced dual estimates as the input estimates converge (Lemmas 5 and 3), using perturbation arguments from Bonnans and Shapiro [7], Bonnans and Shapiro [6], Rockafellar and Wets [34]. The empirical checks appear in Section D.6. For our estimator, these optimization estimates enter only the standard error; they do not enter a separate correction to the point estimate. Their consistency is therefore sufficient, with no additional rate requirement.

The derivative determines how uncertainty in the estimated equalities combines with uncertainty in the objective. The source influence function combines both contributions, so its variance retains their covariance. An independent target sample contributes a separate variance term. We impose the following sampling conditions for these joint expansions.

Assumption C (Sampling and overlap).

The source observations are i.i.d. from PP. In the sampled-target design, the target covariates are i.i.d. from QTQ_{T} and independent of the source sample. In the known-law design, QTQ_{T} is fixed and target integrals are evaluated exactly. Treatment probabilities are known and bounded away from zero. The density ratio w=d​QT/d​PXw=dQ_{T}/dP_{X} exists. The source sites have fixed support {c1,…,cS}\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{S}\}, each relevant site probability is positive, and the covariance of BC⊤​{C−mC​(X)}B_{C}^{\top}\{C-m_{C}(X)\} has its smallest eigenvalue bounded away from zero. For some q>4q>4, the pseudo-outcomes, site-level basis, density ratio, and influence functions in (4.13) and (4.14) have finite qqth moments.

The eigenvalue condition keeps the source moments at the required rank, while the q>4q>4 moment condition controls the nuisance remainders and permits a two-sample central limit theorem.

Debiasing must remove first-order nuisance error from the equality constraints as well as the objective. Once their scores are orthogonal, applying the derivative leaves products of nuisance estimation errors as the remaining bias. Cross-fitting evaluates each score on observations independent of the nuisance estimates, avoiding Donsker conditions on the fitted function classes. The next assumption makes these products negligible relative to n−1/2n^{-1/2}; it imposes no comparable rate on the optimizer or dual estimates.

Assumption D (Nuisance rates for plug-in debiasing).

Conditional on each training sample of the cross-fitting scheme in Section 4.2, the true and estimated nuisance functions are uniformly bounded in Lq​(P)L_{q}(P) and the cross-fitted estimates are consistent in L2​(P)L_{2}(P). In addition, the marginal μ^a​(X)\widehat{\mu}_{a}(X) and m^C\widehat{m}_{C} are consistent in L2​(QT)L_{2}(Q_{T}) and uniformly bounded in Lq​(QT)L_{q}(Q_{T}). Norms of μa\mu_{a} below refer to its marginal form. Norms below are under PP unless marked otherwise. The source errors satisfy

∥w^−w∥2(∥μ^0−μ0∥2+∥μ^1−μ1∥2+∥m^C−mC∥2)=op(n−1/2),∥m^C−mC∥22=op(n−1/2),∥m^C−mC∥2∥μ^a−μa∥2=op(n−1/2)\begin{split}&\|\widehat{w}-w\|_{2}\left(\|\widehat{\mu}_{0}-\mu_{0}\|_{2}+\|\widehat{\mu}_{1}-\mu_{1}\|_{2}+\|\widehat{m}_{C}-m_{C}\|_{2}\right)=o_{p}(n^{-1/2}),\\ &\|\widehat{m}_{C}-m_{C}\|_{2}^{2}=o_{p}(n^{-1/2}),\qquad\|\widehat{m}_{C}-m_{C}\|_{2}\|\widehat{\mu}_{a}-\mu_{a}\|_{2}=o_{p}(n^{-1/2})\end{split} (5.3)

for a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}. It is sufficient that m^C\widehat{m}_{C}, the marginal μ^0,μ^1\widehat{\mu}_{0},\widehat{\mu}_{1}, and w^\widehat{w} each converge at rate op(n−1/4)o_{p}(n^{-1/4}). The joint outcome regressions μ^a​(X,C)\widehat{\mu}_{a}(X,C) need only be consistent, and no rate is imposed on the estimated optimizer or dual variable beyond op​(1)o_{p}(1).

Applying (5.2) to the cross-fitted input expansions gives the source and target influence functions in (4.13) and (4.14). In particular, the dual-weighted source terms account for the movement of the estimated equality constraints; omitting them would generally give an incorrect asymptotic variance. When the restriction set is a finite union of polyhedra, Assumption E ensures that the polyhedron attaining each partial identification bound is locally unchanged (Lemma 3), so the same expansion applies. For sampled target covariates, let nT/n→ζ∈(0,∞]n_{T}/n\to\zeta\in(0,\infty]; ζ=∞\zeta=\infty covers a target sample large relative to the source sample.

Suppose Assumptions A, C, B and D hold and let j∈{−,+}j\in\{-,+\} index the two partial identification bounds. For a polyhedral restriction, our estimator v^jpd\widehat{v}^{\textsc{pd}}_{j} (Algorithm 1) satisfies

The theorem establishes Gaussian inference while accounting for sampling error in the estimated feasible set. The Wald intervals in Section 4.3 incorporate the contribution of the equality constraints through consistently estimated dual weights, without requiring a unique full dual solution or a convergence rate for the optimization estimates beyond consistency. For the partial identification bound functional of the original moments, ϕj\phi_{j} and ϕT,j\phi_{T,j} are the canonical gradients when the observed source law is unrestricted apart from known randomization probabilities and fixed support of site-level variables, and the target covariate law is unrestricted. The variance in Theorem 1 is therefore the minimum asymptotic variance among regular estimators in this observed-data model.

6 Case study: microcredit across countries

We now return to the seven microcredit experiments of Meager [26]. To illustrate our method we select one of the seven countries as a target site whose program characteristics and household covariates are observed but whose experimental outcomes are not. The other six experiments serve as source sites. We estimate the target effect from them and consult the held-out experiment only afterward. This leave-one-country-out exercise asks what a policymaker could have concluded before the target experiment reported its results.

We illustrate our framework on Bosnia and Morocco. These two sites have similar ground truth effects—positive effects on household revenues: 79.879.8 revenue units in Bosnia and 80.980.9 in Morocco—yet vary substantially in terms of their similarity to the rest of the sites. We shall see how our sensitivity approach can show whether a conclusion’s external validity is anchored in observed cross-site variation or in extrapolation assumptions, and how sensitive it is to the choice of source sites. In particular, our method flags the inability to extrapolate in the case of Morocco, and provides some initial evidence that data from other sites can inform the treatment effect in Bosnia.

6.1 Empirical design

We use household revenues on the cross-site consistent scale supplied with the study archive. Unit-level covariates include age, gender, household size, and indicators for no formal education, prior business ownership, and urban residence. We standardize these variables within each site. The site-level variables contain promotion type, annual percentage rate (APR), and average loan size as a share of income, together with their squares and pairwise interactions. We replace each continuous term with its rank among the six source sites and center the ranks at the source site median. This produces p=9p=9 site-level coefficients. We use three-fold cross-fitting, XGBoost nuisance fits, and a regularized multinomial site classifier for mCm_{C}. We aggregate influence-function standard errors at each country’s randomization unit.

The six source-site profiles provide only five independent directions of site-level variables. The covariance matrix ΣC\Sigma_{C} has rank 55 for both targets, leaving exactly four combinations of the nine coefficients in each treatment arm unidentified. To assess how far each target extends beyond the observed site variation, we subtract the mean source-site profile from its target profile. The component outside the source-site span accounts for 89% of this difference vector’s length for Morocco and 46% for Bosnia. This geometric diagnostic shows that Morocco requires more extrapolation beyond the observed site variation. The parameter restrictions determine how much the unidentified coefficient combinations can change the target effect.

We consider three parameter restrictions. First, we impose the magnitude cap on ‖β‖∞\|\beta\|_{\infty} given by one standard deviation of the outcome. Each basis column is scaled by its standard deviation across the source sites, so the cap has the same interpretation across site-level coefficients. Second, we restrict the coefficients on the APR term and the APR interactions in the treatment shift β1−β0\beta_{1}-\beta_{0} to be nonpositive, while leaving the coefficient on APR2\mathrm{APR}^{2} and the control arm unrestricted. At the median source-site profile, this says that an increase in the cost of credit does not raise the benefit of access to credit. Third, we impose effect hierarchy at κ=1\kappa=1. This states that within each treatment arm, every higher-order coefficient must be no larger in magnitude than every direct coefficient. This restriction can sharply limit the interaction terms when one direct effect is close to zero.

For each specification, we ask whether any coefficient vector satisfies both the pooled estimated source equations and these parameter restrictions. We call the optimization problem feasible when such a vector exists and infeasible otherwise. Our estimator (Algorithm 1) preserves the rank of the source equations and pools before optimization, but it cannot ensure that the pooled equations are compatible with the chosen restrictions. Sampling and nuisance estimation errors can change this compatibility.

6.2 What the source experiments support

Figure 3 follows the same restriction order for Bosnia and Morocco. The magnitude cap alone leaves both signs unresolved. The APR sign restriction reduces the Bosnia width by 8.9% and the Morocco width by 30.3%. Neither interval has a fixed sign at this step. Effect hierarchy is the decisive step for Bosnia. It reduces the remaining width by 97.9%, from 4389.54389.5 to 90.290.2, and gives [37.1, 127.3][37.1,\,127.3]. This interval is positive and contains the held-out estimate of 79.879.8. In Morocco, effect hierarchy reduces the remaining width by only 1.1% and gives [−1653.1, 4763.4][-1653.1,\,4763.4]. The APR sign restriction therefore accounts for most of Morocco’s limited reduction. Effect hierarchy has the largest effect in Bosnia.

The positive estimated identified set for Bosnia does not establish a positive effect with statistical confidence. After all three restrictions, the outer limits of the pointwise 95% intervals for its lower and upper partial identification bounds are [−1069.6, 1407.0][-1069.6,\,1407.0], which include zero. The estimates also depend on how observations are partitioned for cross-fitting. In four of seven partitions, no coefficient vector satisfies both the pooled estimated source equations and the restrictions. In the other three, the estimated identified set is positive, with lower partial identification bounds from 0.30.3 to 37.137.1. These checks show that the positive conclusion depends on the estimated equations being compatible with the restrictions and remains subject to substantial sampling uncertainty. Morocco’s interval contains zero in the same checks.

In the top row of Figure 4, we find that the Bosnia result depends on the reported version of effect hierarchy. Under the reported rule, we compare every higher-order term with every direct term in the same treatment arm. This rule reduces the width by 97.4% and gives the positive interval [37.1, 163.1][37.1,\,163.1] before we add the APR sign restriction. If effect hierarchy is applied in a parent-specific style, where the restriction is only applied to interactions against their “parent” direct terms (i.e., |βAPR×Loan|≤|βAPR||\beta_{\mathrm{APR\times Loan}}|\leq|\beta_{\mathrm{APR}}| and |βAPR×Loan|≤|βLoan||\beta_{\mathrm{APR\times Loan}}|\leq|\beta_{\mathrm{Loan}}| only), the width is reduced by only 4.3% and the sign remains unresolved.

In the lower panels, we identify which comparisons produce this change. In Bosnia, direct APR is the smallest direct coefficient in both arms at both endpoints. It therefore sets the limit for every higher-order term. This use of APR is separate from the APR sign restriction in Figure 3. Here we use the magnitude of the APR coefficient as a limit, but we do not restrict its sign. Promotion by loan size has the largest average share of the width change among the higher-order terms, at −40.2%-40.2\%. The effect hierarchy principle compares this interaction with direct APR even though APR is not part of the interaction. Under a parent-specific rule, we would not make this comparison, which explains why the parent-specific rule does not identify a sign. Overall, this indicates that if we believe that interaction terms are dominated by direct effects, then the Bosnia result is supported by the data. When the comparison is limited to parent direct effects, the sign remains unresolved.

Morocco is different. The reported rule reduces its width by only 33.633.6 revenue units, or 0.4%0.4\%. The control and treatment coefficients can move together while their difference changes very little. We use this difference to calculate the target treatment effect, so the interval also changes very little. In the lower right panel, direct APR and loan size each have a share of −50%-50\% of this small reduction. Promotion has a share of zero. In these bars, we assign the reduction across the direct terms that set the effect hierarchy limits. The bars do not describe the APR sign restriction. The Bosnia result therefore depends on the strong comparison across all pairs of terms.

6.3 Practical guidance and robustness checks

Sensitivity analysis should take care to separate conclusions driven by data from those that come solely from assumptions. We recommend a set of best practices that range from rigorous procedural guidelines to additional robustness checks that help evaluate the extent to which conclusions are sensitive to model assumptions and guard against overzealous use of the mathematical programming framework.

We recommend assessing each restriction against a common baseline before combining restrictions. This distinguishes conclusions supported by a single assumption from those that require several assumptions jointly. Adding restrictions one at a time and reporting the bounds at each step produces a ladder that shows what each restriction contributes. Figure 3 provides an example of such a ladder, using the magnitude cap as the baseline restriction. Of course, the contribution of each restriction in this ladder may depend on which restrictions have already been imposed. To that end, we also recommend reconstructing the ladder with different orderings of the restrictions to see how the contribution of each restriction changes. Additionally, restrictions and plausible ranges for sensitivity parameters should be chosen before running the analysis. Ideally, these parameters should be chosen with a substantive justification in mind. For instance, the magnitude cap in Figure 3 is generated from one standard deviation of revenues. Other recommendations include reporting results across the chosen sensitivity range, including where conclusions change, rather than selecting a single favorable specification.

More complex restrictions also warrant examining their constituent parts. The mathematical programming framework lends itself to conducting such comparisons through varying the set of constraints. Figure 4 illustrates this approach for effect hierarchy; for aggregate budgets, one could relax the budget weights on selected groups of terms and recompute the bounds. Throughout these comparisons, the site variables, standardizations, and other parameters should remain fixed so that changes can be attributed to the restriction being examined. Infeasible and unbounded specifications should also be reported, as they reveal where restrictions conflict with the estimated evidence or leave target extrapolations uncontrolled.

Additional robustness checks can vary other aspects of the model or data to assess the stability of the conclusions. Figure 5 considers how changes in the underlying source data and target profile affect the identified set. The top panel asks whether one source experiment is dispensable for the Bosnia conclusion. We remove each source site in turn while holding the source rank transformation, target profile, and restriction set at their values from the full set of six source sites. Every removal lowers the span rank from five to four and produces an interval that contains zero. No removal reverses the sign. Instead, the intervals become too wide to determine it. Bosnia’s positive identified set therefore uses variation contributed by all six source sites. Reporting the results for each subset of source sites helps researchers understand how much the conclusion depends on the observed source variation and can be especially important when the number of source sites is small.

The lower panels ask whether the result is an accident of Bosnia’s program terms. We move its APR and loan size ranks across the full range observed at the source sites, holding the source data and all other target features fixed. The identified set stays positive at all 21 APR values and at 16 of 21 loan size values. It loses the sign only toward the upper end of the loan size range, far from Bosnia’s observed program, whose loan size lies near the bottom of the source site distribution. Thus, modest changes to Bosnia’s target profile do not explain the result. Rather, the diversity of source sites does. This check can help assess how sensitive conclusions are to the target profile.

In our application, we find that in Bosnia effect hierarchy yields positive estimated bounds that persist across plausible changes to the target profile. However, the result depends on every source site and is primarily driven by the effect hierarchy assumption applied to interaction terms. The program is infeasible in four of seven sample splits, and sampling uncertainty remains large. In Morocco, the same restrictions leave the sign unresolved. These checks clarify which assumptions and source evidence a conclusion depends on, and where the available information remains insufficient.

7 Discussion

External validity cannot be established in general from source experiments alone. Learning about a new setting requires assumptions about how treatment effects change across settings, leaving practitioners with an uncomfortable choice: trust the source effects to carry over or give up on drawing a conclusion about the target. We believe sensitivity analysis provides a middle ground. Researchers can state which departures from the source settings they consider plausible and examine which conclusions survive those departures.

Our approach is one way to turn a modeler’s substantive prior beliefs and domain knowledge into quantifiable partial identification bounds. Parameter restrictions describe which responses to changes in sites are plausible; the source experiments then limit the target effects consistent with those restrictions. Varying the restrictions makes their role in a conclusion explicit. A conclusion that persists across plausible specifications has a different evidential basis from one that requires a particular assumption. The restrictions we study illustrate this use of sensitivity analysis, but many other ways of representing knowledge about external validity remain possible.

Developing useful parameter restrictions requires practitioners who understand the mechanisms through which site-level variables change treatment effects. Different applications may call for restrictions on the direction or magnitude of those changes, or on how site-level features interact. Source experiments and observational data could inform both the form and the strength of these restrictions. Developing such restrictions, assessing their substantive credibility, and accounting for uncertainty when they are informed by data are promising directions for future research. This work would make sensitivity analysis more useful by connecting what practitioners know about an intervention to what they can conclude in a new setting.
