Appendix A Normal equations and identification of the target effect

We characterize the coefficients that reproduce the source conditional means, then determine which target effects those coefficients permit. This proves the normal equations (3.7) and Corollary 1. Under the sensitivity restrictions, the same characterization gives the exact target-effect set. Proofs of the supporting results appear in the subsections below.

A.1 From the source equations to the target-effect set

Profiling the unrestricted regression function leaves only variation in context conditional on XX. The following lemma characterizes what this variation identifies. We assume throughout that the stated second moments are finite. Write C~=C−mC​(X)\widetilde{C}=C-m_{C}(X) and da=𝔼P​[Cov⁡(C,Ra∣X)]=P⁡{C~​(Ua−μa​(X))}d_{a}=\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C,R_{a}\mid X)]=P\{\widetilde{C}(U_{a}-\mu_{a}(X))\} for the source cross-moment in (3.7).

Lemma 1 (Profiled loss and source-compatible coefficients).

For each arm aa and coefficient β\beta, the profiled minimizer is fa,β​(x)=μa​(x)−mC​(x)⊤​βf_{a,\beta}(x)=\mu_{a}(x)-m_{C}(x)^{\top}\beta. The coefficients minimizing the profiled loss are exactly the solutions of ΣC​β=da\Sigma_{C}\beta=d_{a}, and da∈range⁡(ΣC)d_{a}\in\rangeop(\Sigma_{C}). Under the response model (A), these are exactly the coefficients for which

fa,β​(X)+C⊤​β=μa​(X,C)P​-almost surely.f_{a,\beta}(X)+C^{\top}\beta=\mu_{a}(X,C)\quad P\text{-almost surely}.

Proof in Appendix A.2.

Lemma 1 gives (3.7). To determine the target effect, impose target response invariance,

𝔼⁡[YT​(a)∣XT=x]=ga​(x)+cT⊤​βa,a∈{0,1},\mathbb{E}[Y_{T}(a)\mid X_{T}=x]=g_{a}(x)+c_{T}^{\top}\beta_{a},\qquad a\in\{0,1\}, (A.1)

and QT≪PXQ_{T}\ll P_{X}. Substituting the profiled functions into this target mean gives

ψT=QT​(μ1−μ0)+{cT−QT​mC}⊤​(β1−β0)=bT+ℓT⊤​(β1−β0).\psi_{T}=Q_{T}(\mu_{1}-\mu_{0})+\{c_{T}-Q_{T}m_{C}\}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0})=b_{T}+\ell_{T}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}).

Thus the remaining identification question is whether the source equations fix this linear functional of the coefficients.

To prove Corollary 1, use da∈range⁡(ΣC)d_{a}\in\rangeop(\Sigma_{C}), so ΣC​ΣC+​da=da\Sigma_{C}\Sigma_{C}^{+}d_{a}=d_{a}. Thus, ΣC+​da\Sigma_{C}^{+}d_{a} is one solution, and subtracting it from any other solution gives an element of ker⁡(ΣC)\kernelop(\Sigma_{C}). Consequently, {βa:ΣC​βa=da}=ΣC+​da+ker⁡(ΣC)\{\beta_{a}:\Sigma_{C}\beta_{a}=d_{a}\}=\Sigma_{C}^{+}d_{a}+\kernelop(\Sigma_{C}). Substitution into the target effect gives

ψT=bT+ℓT⊤​ΣC+​(d1−d0)+ℓT⊤​(z1−z0).\psi_{T}=b_{T}+\ell_{T}^{\top}\Sigma_{C}^{+}(d_{1}-d_{0})+\ell_{T}^{\top}(z_{1}-z_{0}).

The final term vanishes for every z0,z1∈ker⁡(ΣC)z_{0},z_{1}\in\kernelop(\Sigma_{C}) exactly when ℓT∈ker⁡(ΣC)⟂=range⁡(ΣC)\ell_{T}\in\kernelop(\Sigma_{C})^{\perp}=\rangeop(\Sigma_{C}). If this condition fails, choose z∈ker⁡(ΣC)z\in\kernelop(\Sigma_{C}) with ℓT⊤​z≠0\ell_{T}^{\top}z\neq 0 and replace β1\beta_{1} by β1+t​z\beta_{1}+tz. Each pair therefore reproduces the same source conditional means by Lemma 1. The target effect ranges over ℝ\mathbb{R} as tt varies.

The range condition has a direct interpretation in terms of the observed site profiles. Recall 𝒱C=span⁡{cs−c1:s≥2}\mathcal{V}_{C}=\operatorname{span}\{c_{s}-c_{1}:s\geq 2\} and its orthonormal basis BCB_{C}.

Both C−c1C-c_{1} and its conditional expectation given XX lie in 𝒱C\mathcal{V}_{C}, so C~∈𝒱C\widetilde{C}\in\mathcal{V}_{C} almost surely. Writing Z=BC⊤​C~Z=B_{C}^{\top}\widetilde{C} gives C~=BC​Z\widetilde{C}=B_{C}Z and ΣC=BC​P​(Z​Z⊤)​BC⊤\Sigma_{C}=B_{C}P(ZZ^{\top})B_{C}^{\top}. Consequently,

range⁡(ΣC)⊆𝒱C,rank⁡(ΣC)≤r≤S−1,da∈𝒱C.\rangeop(\Sigma_{C})\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{C},\qquad\rankop(\Sigma_{C})\leq r\leq S-1,\qquad d_{a}\in\mathcal{V}_{C}. (A.2)

Under (B.4), P⁡(Z​Z⊤)=Ω≻0P(ZZ^{\top})=\Omega\succ 0, so

ΣC=BC​Ω​BC⊤,range⁡(ΣC)=𝒱C,ker⁡(ΣC)=𝒱C⟂.\Sigma_{C}=B_{C}\Omega B_{C}^{\top},\qquad\rangeop(\Sigma_{C})=\mathcal{V}_{C},\qquad\kernelop(\Sigma_{C})=\mathcal{V}_{C}^{\perp}. (A.3)

To translate the range condition into a condition on the target profile, let ps​(x)=P⁡(C=cs∣X=x)p_{s}(x)=P(C=c_{s}\mid X=x). Covariate overlap gives

c¯:=QT​mC=∑s=1Scs​QT​ps∈conv⁡{c1,…,cS}⊆c1+𝒱C.\bar{c}:=Q_{T}m_{C}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}c_{s}Q_{T}p_{s}\in\convop\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{S}\}\subseteq c_{1}+\mathcal{V}_{C}.

Since ℓT=cT−c¯\ell_{T}=c_{T}-\bar{c} and range⁡(ΣC)=𝒱C\rangeop(\Sigma_{C})=\mathcal{V}_{C}, we obtain

ℓT∈range(ΣC)⟺cT∈aff{c1,…,cS}.\ell_{T}\in\rangeop(\Sigma_{C})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad c_{T}\in\affop\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{S}\}. (A.4)

By Corollary 1, the unrestricted target effect is therefore bT+ℓT⊤​ΣC+​(d1−d0)b_{T}+\ell_{T}^{\top}\Sigma_{C}^{+}(d_{1}-d_{0}) when the target profile lies in this affine span, and is unbounded in both directions otherwise. In particular, it is point identified whenever cTc_{T} is a realized source profile.

When this condition fails, sensitivity restrictions limit the coefficient directions that the source cannot identify. Intersecting the normal equations with ℛ\mathcal{R} gives ℱ\mathcal{F}. The following proposition shows that projecting this feasible set produces exactly the target effects compatible with the model.

Proposition 2 (Exact projection and mean sharpness).

Assume the response model (A), target response invariance (A.1), unrestricted support for the potential outcomes, and that ℱ\mathcal{F} is nonempty. The exact target-effect set is

ℐT={bT+ℓT⊤​(β1−β0):β∈ℱ}.\mathcal{I}_{T}=\{b_{T}+\ell_{T}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}):\beta\in\mathcal{F}\}. (A.5)

Every value in this set is attained by a source-target response model that leaves the observed source law unchanged. Each polyhedral branch of ℱ\mathcal{F} projects to an interval, possibly empty, unbounded, or a singleton. A finite union projects to a finite union of such intervals, and [v−,v+][v_{-},v_{+}] is its convex hull. For a convex restriction, the exact set equals this interval. Proof in Appendix A.3.

Consequently, the optimization problems in (3.12) give the sharp lower and upper bounds. For a finite union, the branchwise intervals retain any gaps in the exact set; the two outer bounds describe its convex hull.

A.2 Proof of Lemma 1

Fix an arm aa and a coefficient vector β\beta. Conditional expectation is the L2L_{2} projection on functions of XX, so profiling ff from E​{Ra−f⁡(X)−C⊤​β}2E\{R_{a}-f(X)-C^{\top}\beta\}^{2} gives

f⁡(x)=μa​(x)−E​(C∣X=x)⊤​β.f(x)=\mu_{a}(x)-E(C\mid X=x)^{\top}\beta.

The residual context is

mC​(x)=𝔼P​[C∣X=x],C~=C−mC​(X),m_{C}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{P}[C\mid X=x],\qquad\widetilde{C}=C-m_{C}(X), (A.6)

and the source moments are

ΣC=P⁡(C~​C~⊤),da=P⁡{C~​(Ua−μa​(X))}.\Sigma_{C}=P(\widetilde{C}\widetilde{C}^{\top}),\qquad d_{a}=P\{\widetilde{C}(U_{a}-\mu_{a}(X))\}. (A.7)

Throughout the appendices, ΣC\Sigma_{C} and dad_{a} abbreviate the covariances written in operator form in the main text: because C~\widetilde{C} is centered, ΣC=𝔼P​[Cov⁡(C∣X)]\Sigma_{C}=\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C\mid X)] and da=𝔼P​[Cov⁡(C,Ra∣X)]d_{a}=\mathbb{E}_{P}[{\rm Cov}(C,R_{a}\mid X)]. The moment dad_{a} is unchanged if UaU_{a} is replaced by RaR_{a}. After profiling, the part of the loss that depends on β\beta is

−2​β⊤​da+β⊤​ΣC​β.-2\beta^{\top}d_{a}+\beta^{\top}\Sigma_{C}\beta.

Its normal equation is therefore ΣC​β=da\Sigma_{C}\beta=d_{a}.

For completeness, ΣC\Sigma_{C} is positive semidefinite because

z⊤​ΣC​z=E⁡{(z⊤​C~)2}≥0.z^{\top}\Sigma_{C}z=E\{(z^{\top}\widetilde{C})^{2}\}\geq 0. (A.8)

If z∈ker⁡(ΣC)z\in\kernelop(\Sigma_{C}), then z⊤​C~=0z^{\top}\widetilde{C}=0 almost surely and hence z⊤​da=0z^{\top}d_{a}=0. Thus da∈range⁡(ΣC)d_{a}\in\rangeop(\Sigma_{C}), using

range⁡(ΣC)=ker⁡(ΣC)⟂\rangeop(\Sigma_{C})=\kernelop(\Sigma_{C})^{\perp}

for a symmetric matrix. Completing the quadratic around any solution shows that the minimizers are exactly the solutions of the normal equation.

Randomization and consistency imply

𝔼P[Ra∣X,C]=μa(X,C)=ga0(X)+C⊤βa0\mathbb{E}_{P}[R_{a}\mid X,C]=\mu_{a}(X,C)=g_{a}^{0}(X)+C^{\top}\beta_{a}^{0} (A.9)

da=P⁡{C~​(μa​(X,C)−μa​(X))}=P⁡(C~​C~⊤)​βa0=ΣC​βa0.\begin{split}d_{a}&=P\{\widetilde{C}(\mu_{a}(X,C)-\mu_{a}(X))\}\\ &=P(\widetilde{C}\widetilde{C}^{\top})\beta_{a}^{0}=\Sigma_{C}\beta_{a}^{0}.\end{split} (A.11)

ga​(X)+C⊤​β=μa​(X)+C~⊤​β=μa​(X)+C~⊤​βa0=μa​(X,C)\begin{split}g_{a}(X)+C^{\top}\beta=\mu_{a}(X)+\widetilde{C}^{\top}\beta=\mu_{a}(X)+\widetilde{C}^{\top}\beta_{a}^{0}=\mu_{a}(X,C)\end{split} (A.12)

The argument uses only E(Ra∣X,C)=E{Y(a)∣X,C}E(R_{a}\mid X,C)=E\{Y(a)\mid X,C\}, so it also applies when the known, positive assignment probability varies with (X,C)(X,C).

A.3 Proof of Proposition 2

We prove necessity and attainability separately.

Necessity.

Consider any source-target response model admitted by the assumptions and the restriction ℛ\mathcal{R}. Its coefficients satisfy ΣC​βa=da\Sigma_{C}\beta_{a}=d_{a} by Lemma 1. They also satisfy β∈ℛ\beta\in\mathcal{R} by construction. Hence β∈ℱ\beta\in\mathcal{F}. Target response invariance (A.1) and (3.4) then imply

𝔼⁡{YT​(1)−YT​(0)}=bT+ℓT⊤​(β1−β0).\mathbb{E}\{Y_{T}(1)-Y_{T}(0)\}=b_{T}+\ell_{T}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}). (A.13)

Every admissible target effect therefore belongs to the right side of (A.5).

Attainability.

Fix an arbitrary β∈ℱ\beta\in\mathcal{F} and define

ga​(x)=μa​(x)−mC​(x)⊤​βa.g_{a}(x)=\mu_{a}(x)-m_{C}(x)^{\top}\beta_{a}. (A.14)

Because ΣC​βa=da\Sigma_{C}\beta_{a}=d_{a} for both arms, Lemma 1 gives

ga​(X)+C⊤​βa=μa​(X,C)P​-almost surely,g_{a}(X)+C^{\top}\beta_{a}=\mu_{a}(X,C)\quad P\text{-almost surely}, (A.15)

on the source support.

We now construct a full source potential-outcome law. Let

Fa​(ℬ∣x,c)=P⁡(Y∈ℬ∣A=a,X=x,C=c)F_{a}(\mathcal{B}\mid x,c)=P(Y\in\mathcal{B}\mid A=a,X=x,C=c) (A.16)

denote the observed conditional outcome law in arm aa. Draw (X,C)(X,C) from its observed source marginal. Conditional on (X,C)=(x,c)(X,C)=(x,c), draw (Y⁡(0),Y⁡(1))(Y(0),Y(1)) from any coupling whose two marginal laws are F0(⋅∣x,c)F_{0}(\cdot\mid x,c) and F1(⋅∣x,c)F_{1}(\cdot\mid x,c). The conditional product of these laws is one such coupling. Next draw AA independently of (Y⁡(0),Y⁡(1))(Y(0),Y(1)) given (X,C)(X,C), using the known probabilities ea​(X,C)e_{a}(X,C), and set

Y=A​Y​(1)+(1−A)​Y​(0).Y=AY(1)+(1-A)Y(0). (A.17)

This construction satisfies consistency and conditional randomization. It also preserves the complete observed source law. To see this, for every measurable ℬ\mathcal{B} and each arm aa,

P∗(Y∈ℬ,A=a∣X=x,C=c)=P∗​(A=a∣X=x,C=c)​P∗​(Y⁡(a)∈ℬ∣X=x,C=c)=ea​(x,c)​Fa​(ℬ∣x,c),\begin{split}&P^{*}(Y\in\mathcal{B},A=a\mid X=x,C=c)\\ &\qquad=P^{*}(A=a\mid X=x,C=c)P^{*}(Y(a)\in\mathcal{B}\mid X=x,C=c)\\ &\qquad=e_{a}(x,c)F_{a}(\mathcal{B}\mid x,c),\end{split} (A.18)

which is the corresponding conditional probability under the observed law PP. The marginal law of (X,C)(X,C) was also kept fixed, so P∗=PP^{*}=P on (Y,A,X,C)(Y,A,X,C).

The mean of Fa(⋅∣x,c)F_{a}(\cdot\mid x,c) is μa​(x,c)\mu_{a}(x,c). Therefore the constructed potential outcomes satisfy

𝔼P∗[Y(a)∣X,C]=μa​(X,C)=ga​(X)+C⊤​βa,\begin{split}\mathbb{E}_{P^{*}}[Y(a)\mid X,C]&=\mu_{a}(X,C)\\ &=g_{a}(X)+C^{\top}\beta_{a},\end{split} (A.19)

where the second equality is (A.15). Thus the constructed source law obeys the response model with the chosen coefficient pair even though the observed law is unchanged.

It remains to construct the target law. Draw XT∼QTX_{T}\sim Q_{T}; the function gag_{a} in (A.14) is defined QTQ_{T}-almost everywhere because QT≪PXQ_{T}\ll P_{X}. Define

YT​(a)=ga​(XT)+cT⊤​βa+εa,T,Y_{T}(a)=g_{a}(X_{T})+c_{T}^{\top}\beta_{a}+\varepsilon_{a,T}, (A.20)

where (ε0,T,ε1,T)(\varepsilon_{0,T},\varepsilon_{1,T}) has conditional mean zero given XTX_{T} and finite second moments. One may take both residuals to be zero. The unrestricted outcome-support assumption permits this target construction. Conditional expectation gives, arm by arm,

𝔼⁡[YT​(a)∣XT]=ga​(XT)+cT⊤​βa,\mathbb{E}[Y_{T}(a)\mid X_{T}]=g_{a}(X_{T})+c_{T}^{\top}\beta_{a}, (A.21)

so target response invariance (A.1) holds for the constructed law. Its average treatment effect is

𝔼⁡{YT​(1)−YT​(0)}=QT​(g1−g0)+cT⊤​(β1−β0)=QT​{μ1−μ0−mC⊤​(β1−β0)}+cT⊤​(β1−β0)=QT​(μ1−μ0)+{cT−QT​mC}⊤​(β1−β0)=bT+ℓT⊤​(β1−β0).\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\{Y_{T}(1)-Y_{T}(0)\}&=Q_{T}(g_{1}-g_{0})+c_{T}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0})\\ &=Q_{T}\{\mu_{1}-\mu_{0}-m_{C}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0})\}+c_{T}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0})\\ &=Q_{T}(\mu_{1}-\mu_{0})+\{c_{T}-Q_{T}m_{C}\}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0})\\ &=b_{T}+\ell_{T}^{\top}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{0}).\end{split} (A.22)

The second equality substitutes (A.14); the last equality uses (3.4). Since the initial β∈ℱ\beta\in\mathcal{F} was arbitrary, every value on the right side of (A.5) is attained. Combining this construction with the necessity argument proves equality in (A.5).

Finally, Fourier–Motzkin elimination implies that

{Ψ0+q⊤​x:x∈𝒫}​ is a closed interval, half-line, singleton, ​ℝ, or empty\{\Psi_{0}+q^{\top}x:x\in\mathcal{P}\}\text{ is a closed interval, half-line, singleton, }\mathbb{R},\text{ or empty}

for any polyhedron 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Taking the finite union proves the branch claim. If ℱ\mathcal{F} is convex, its affine image is convex and therefore equals the interval between its two extrema.

Fix an endpoint j∈{−,+}j\in\{-,+\}. We first consider its population-winning polyhedron. and the target gradients by

Lemma 2 (Cross-fitted input expansion).

Under Assumptions C and D, Algorithm 1 satisfies

Γ^−Γ=1n∑i=1nφΓ(Oi)+1nT∑i=1nTφT,Γ(XT,i)+op(n−1/2).\widehat{\Gamma}-\Gamma=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varphi_{\Gamma}(O_{i})+\frac{1}{n_{T}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{T}}\varphi_{T,\Gamma}(X_{T,i})+o_{p}(n^{-1/2}). (B.1)

This restriction is needed because an arbitrary perturbation of the singular full equality system could make it infeasible. The next result gives the change in the optimized value along the perturbations that the estimator actually produces.

Lemma 3 (Derivative of the partial identification bound).

Suppose Assumption B holds for the branch. Its endpoint value vjv_{j} on 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C} is Hadamard differentiable at Γ\Gamma tangentially to the tangent space of 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C}. For a tangent perturbation Γ˙=(b˙,ℓ˙,Σ˙,d˙0,d˙1)\dot{\Gamma}=(\dot{b},\dot{\ell},\dot{\Sigma},\dot{d}_{0},\dot{d}_{1}),

It remains to justify replacing the population influence functions by the reported estimates. In addition to fitted nuisances, these estimates use an optimizer and dual variables computed from the whole moment vector, so their consistency must also be established.

Finite unions.

For a finite union we impose the following branch-separation assumption used in the theorem.

Assumption E (Branch separation for finite unions).

Each endpoint has a unique winning branch and encoding, with a positive population value gap to every other feasible branch. Every competing branch is either locally infeasible or has a locally finite continuous value.

The winning value is continuous by the differentiability just proved. Discard locally infeasible competitors and let Δ>0\Delta>0 be the smallest population gap among those remaining. By continuity, on a sufficiently small common neighborhood every branch value differs from its population value by less than Δ/3\Delta/3. The winner therefore retains a gap of at least Δ/3\Delta/3. If no competitors remain, it is the sole feasible branch throughout a neighborhood. In either case the union value agrees locally with the winning branch and inherits its derivative. A consistent input estimate lies in this neighborhood with probability tending to one, so the union and winning-branch estimators are identical on that event and differ by op(n−1/2)o_{p}(n^{-1/2}). This completes the proof of Lemma 3.

At a tie between optimizers or branches, Gaussian inference can therefore fail unless the tied derivatives agree [17]. Assumption E also imposes local finiteness and continuity of the competitors separately. Fixed polyhedral inequalities and full-row-rank equalities alone do not ensure these properties. For example, with p=2p=2, r=1r=1, BC=(1,0)⊤B_{C}=(1,0)^{\top}, Ω=1\Omega=1, ς0=ς1=0\varsigma_{0}=\varsigma_{1}=0, and restrictions β0,2,β1,2≥0\beta_{0,2},\beta_{1,2}\geq 0, the branch value at b=1b=1 and ℓ=(0,ϵ)⊤\ell=(0,\epsilon)^{\top} is infβ0,2,β1,2≥0{1+ϵ⁡(β1,2−β0,2)}\inf_{\beta_{0,2},\beta_{1,2}\geq 0}\{1+\epsilon(\beta_{1,2}-\beta_{0,2})\}. It equals 11 at ϵ=0\epsilon=0 and −∞-\infty elsewhere. ♢\diamondsuit

{z:H0z=0,Gz≤0,g⊤z≤0}={0}.\{z:H_{0}z=0,\ Gz\leq 0,\ g^{\top}z\leq 0\}=\{0\}. (B.23)

bn+gn⊤​βn≤u⁡(γn)+εn≤bn+gn⊤​β~n+εn.b_{n}+g_{n}^{\top}\beta_{n}\leq u(\gamma_{n})+\varepsilon_{n}\leq b_{n}+g_{n}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{n}+\varepsilon_{n}.

B.3 Proof of Lemma 4

The input expansion gives γ^→pγ∗\widehat{\gamma}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\rightarrow}}\gamma^{*} within the open reduced domain. To prove consistency of the reported variance, we first need convergence of the optimizer and dual variables used in the fitted influence functions.

Proposition 3 (Consistency of reduced KKT selections).

Assume that Assumption B holds. Let γn→γ∗\gamma_{n}\to\gamma^{\ast} in 𝒰\mathcal{U} and let ξn=(βn,λ¯n,νn)\xi_{n}=(\beta_{n},\bar{\lambda}_{n},\nu_{n}) be any measurable selection of KKT triples for γn\gamma_{n}. Then ξn→ξ⋆​(γ∗)\xi_{n}\to\xi^{\star}(\gamma^{\ast}). Proof in Appendix B.3.1.

For a finite union, Lemma 3 places the reported solution on the population-winning branch with probability tending to one. Proposition 3 then gives convergence of the optimizer and reduced dual. The lift λa=BC​λ¯a\lambda_{a}=B_{C}\bar{\lambda}_{a} is fixed and linear, so the minimum-norm full dual converges as well.

We next separate nuisance replacement from replacement of these global optimization estimates. Let ϕ~j,k\tilde{\phi}_{j,k} denote the fold-kk source influence function using fitted nuisances but population coefficients and dual variables. Define ϕ~T,j,k\tilde{\phi}_{T,j,k} analogously. In (4.13), the nuisance errors enter through w^​U~^a−w​U~a\widehat{w}\widehat{\widetilde{U}}_{a}-w\widetilde{U}_{a}, w^​C~^−w​C~\widehat{w}\widehat{\widetilde{C}}-w\widetilde{C}, and

C~^​(U~^a−C~^⊤​βj,a∗)−C~​(U~a−C~⊤​βj,a∗).\widehat{\widetilde{C}}(\widehat{\widetilde{U}}_{a}-\widehat{\widetilde{C}}^{\top}\beta^{*}_{j,a})-\widetilde{C}(\widetilde{U}_{a}-\widetilde{C}^{\top}\beta^{*}_{j,a}).

‖ϕ~j,k−ϕj‖P,2=op​(1),‖ϕ~T,j,k−ϕT,j‖QT,2=op​(1).\|\tilde{\phi}_{j,k}-\phi_{j}\|_{P,2}=o_{p}(1),\qquad\|\tilde{\phi}_{T,j,k}-\phi_{T,j}\|_{Q_{T},2}=o_{p}(1).

For the target function, this follows directly from target L2L_{2} consistency of the marginal regressions. Conditional Markov’s inequality on each holdout now makes the empirical averages of the squared differences op​(1)o_{p}(1). Pooling finitely many folds preserves this conclusion.

The optimizer and dual estimates use the whole sample, so we handle their replacement by a deterministic bound. At fixed fitted nuisances, the source influence function is a finite linear combination of

w^​U~^a,w^​C~^,C~^​U~^a,vec⁡(C~^​C~^⊤).\widehat{w}\widehat{\widetilde{U}}_{a},\qquad\widehat{w}\widehat{\widetilde{C}},\qquad\widehat{\widetilde{C}}\widehat{\widetilde{U}}_{a},\qquad\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\widetilde{C}}\widehat{\widetilde{C}}^{\top}).

The coefficients are continuous functions of the optimizer and dual variables. Their changes are op​(1)o_{p}(1) by the convergence already proved. Each displayed fitted quantity has an Op​(1)O_{p}(1) empirical second moment: its conditional population second moment is Op​(1)O_{p}(1) by the LqL_{q} bounds, and conditional Markov’s inequality transfers this bound to the holdout. Thus, by Cauchy–Schwarz in this finite-dimensional combination, replacing the optimization estimates changes the pooled empirical squared difference by op​(1)o_{p}(1). Combining the two replacements gives

1n​∑i{ϕ^j​(Oi)−ϕj​(Oi)}2=op​(1),1nT​∑i{ϕ^T,j​(XT,i)−ϕT,j​(XT,i)}2=op​(1).\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\{\widehat{\phi}_{j}(O_{i})-\phi_{j}(O_{i})\}^{2}=o_{p}(1),\qquad\frac{1}{n_{T}}\sum_{i}\{\widehat{\phi}_{T,j}(X_{T,i})-\phi_{T,j}(X_{T,i})\}^{2}=o_{p}(1).

Here each fitted function uses the nuisance estimates for that observation’s fold. Cauchy–Schwarz and the ordinary law of large numbers for the population influence functions imply convergence of the empirical first and second moments. Their centered empirical variances consequently converge to the two population variances. Appendix C Effect hierarchy as a finite union of linear optimization problems

We show that effect hierarchy can be imposed exactly by solving finitely many linear programs. We then identify how zero direct coefficients can create tied branches, which prevents the branch-separation condition used for Gaussian inference.

Partition the site-level variables as C=(CD⊤,CH⊤)⊤C=(C_{D}^{\top},C_{H}^{\top})^{\top}, with pDp_{D} direct terms and pHp_{H} higher-order terms, and partition each arm’s coefficients as βa=(βa,D⊤,βa,H⊤)⊤\beta_{a}=(\beta_{a,D}^{\top},\beta_{a,H}^{\top})^{\top}. Effect hierarchy, restriction (2.6) of Section 2, bounds every higher-order coefficient by a multiple of every direct coefficient in the same arm. Given a sensitivity level κ≥0\kappa\geq 0, it requires

|βa,H,j|≤κ​|βa,D,k|for every ​a∈{0,1},j≤pH,k≤pD.|\beta_{a,H,j}|\leq\kappa|\beta_{a,D,k}|\quad\text{for every }a\in\{0,1\},\ j\leq p_{H},\ k\leq p_{D}. (C.1)

The comparison is per arm and over all direct–higher-order pairs. Reporting guidance appears in Section D.7.

C.1 Exact representation and local branch selection

For each arm aa and direct term kk, choose a sign ωa,k∈{−1,1}\omega_{a,k}\in\{-1,1\}. On that branch impose

ωa,k​βa,D,k\displaystyle\omega_{a,k}\beta_{a,D,k} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0, (C.2)
βa,H,j\displaystyle\beta_{a,H,j} ≤κ​ωa,k​βa,D,k,\displaystyle\leq\kappa\omega_{a,k}\beta_{a,D,k}, (C.3)
−βa,H,j\displaystyle-\beta_{a,H,j} ≤κ​ωa,k​βa,D,k\displaystyle\leq\kappa\omega_{a,k}\beta_{a,D,k} (C.4)

for every higher-order term jj and every direct term kk. Conditional on (C.2), the right-hand side equals κ​|βa,D,k|\kappa|\beta_{a,D,k}|. Thus (C.3)–(C.4) are exactly |βa,H,j|≤κ​|βa,D,k||\beta_{a,H,j}|\leq\kappa|\beta_{a,D,k}|. Each sign pattern ω=(ωa,k)\omega=(\omega_{a,k}) therefore contributes one polyhedron F⁡(ω)={β:Gω​β≤hω}F(\omega)=\{\beta:G_{\omega}\beta\leq h_{\omega}\} of the finite union (B.8), with (Gω,hω)(G_{\omega},h_{\omega}) fixed by the analyst and not varying with γ\gamma, as Assumption B requires.

Every coefficient vector satisfying effect hierarchy has a compatible sign pattern, obtained from its direct coefficients; a zero coefficient may use either sign. Conversely, on any branch, ωa,k​βa,D,k=|βa,D,k|\omega_{a,k}\beta_{a,D,k}=|\beta_{a,D,k}|, so its inequalities imply (C.1). Hence the effect-hierarchy set equals the union over all 22​pD2^{2p_{D}} arm-specific direct-sign patterns. Intersecting each branch with the source normal equations gives polyhedra whose union is exactly the original feasible set. Enumeration is practical when pDp_{D} is small. For each sign pattern, solve the lower and upper linear optimization problems, discard infeasible branches, and retain both the outer partial identification bound and the second-best branch value. Recording the branchwise intervals also reveals whether the exact projection set has gaps.

C.2 When enumeration creates a tie

At a zero direct coefficient, the same optimizer can have two sign encodings. To see this, orient the endpoint as a minimization, let ω\omega be a winning pattern with optimizer β⋆\beta^{\star}, and suppose βa,D,k⋆=0\beta^{\star}_{a,D,k}=0. The branch inequalities imply |βa,H,j⋆|≤κ​|βa,D,k⋆|=0|\beta^{\star}_{a,H,j}|\leq\kappa|\beta^{\star}_{a,D,k}|=0 for every jj, so βa,H⋆=0\beta^{\star}_{a,H}=0. Flipping only ωa,k\omega_{a,k} gives a pattern ω′\omega^{\prime} whose changed inequalities still hold with equality at β⋆\beta^{\star}. Thus β⋆∈F⁡(ω′)\beta^{\star}\in F(\omega^{\prime}) and u⁡(ω′)≤u⁡(ω)u(\omega^{\prime})\leq u(\omega). Since ω\omega attains the winning value, the two values coincide and β⋆\beta^{\star} is optimal on both branches. Conversely, feasibility under both signs forces ωa,k​βa,D,k≥0\omega_{a,k}\beta_{a,D,k}\geq 0 and −ωa,k​βa,D,k≥0-\omega_{a,k}\beta_{a,D,k}\geq 0, hence βa,D,k=0\beta_{a,D,k}=0.

The same argument applies when several zero coordinates are flipped. Thus

mina∈{0,1},k≤pD⁡|βa,D,k⋆|>0\min_{a\in\{0,1\},\,k\leq p_{D}}|\beta^{\star}_{a,D,k}|>0 (C.5)

makes the optimizer feasible under exactly one sign encoding. Local selection also requires the positive gap to every other feasible branch and the competitor continuity required by Assumption E.

A shared population optimizer does not imply that tied branch value maps have the same derivative. An arbitrarily small perturbation can select different branches. Unless their derivatives are proved to agree, such a tie does not establish ordinary Hadamard differentiability of the union value. The Gaussian result in Theorem 1 uses Assumption E to exclude ties through a unique winning encoding and a positive gap.

Nothing in this construction is specific to effect hierarchy. Any restriction written as a finite union of polyhedra with fixed (Gω,hω)(G_{\omega},h_{\omega}) enters the theory in the same way, through one branch program per polyhedron together with the checks of Assumptions B and E.

Remark 2 (The per-arm, all-pairs convention): Two design choices in (C.1) deserve emphasis, because natural variants exist. The comparison is per arm and over all pairs (j,k)(j,k), so each higher-order coefficient is bounded by κ\kappa times the smallest direct magnitude of its arm; a parent-specific variant, indexing kk over the parents of interaction jj only, is strictly weaker. And the aggregate family (2.7) is likewise written per arm; writing it on the contrast block β1−β0\beta_{1}-\beta_{0} with a single index map would produce a different set. The paper adopts the per-arm, all-pairs forms throughout and the case study says so when interpreting them. ♢\diamondsuit

The two source contexts (0,0)(0,0) and (1,1)(1,1) identify τ0\tau_{0} and ρ=θ1+θ2\rho=\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}. Centering the two profiles gives a covariance proportional to

[1111],\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 1&1\end{bmatrix}, (D.2)

whose range is span⁡(1,1)\operatorname{span}(1,1) and whose null space is span⁡(1,−1)\operatorname{span}(1,-1). The affine fiber is (θ1,θ2)=(t,ρ−t)(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})=(t,\rho-t). The optimization problem is infeasible if |ρ|>2​M|\rho|>2M, unbounded without the box, and point identified for the on-span target. The span, rather than the convex hull, is the relevant geometry under the linear response model.

D.2 The standard one-step correction

The standard one-step correction (Algorithm 2) is the benchmark used in Section 4.4. On each fold it solves the partial identification bound program at a fitted, uncorrected input and adds the held-out mean of the influence function. Write Γ^pl,(k)\widehat{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{pl},(k)} for that fitted input, ξ^(k)\widehat{\xi}^{(k)} for its optimizer and dual variables, and v⁡(Γ^pl,(k))v(\widehat{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{pl},(k)}) for its lower value. Here nkn_{k} is the source fold size, ℙn,k\mathbb{P}_{n,k} and ℚT,k\mathbb{Q}_{T,k} average over the held-out source and target folds, and ϕ,ϕT\phi,\phi_{T} are the influence functions derived in Section 4.3. The lower endpoint is

v^−os=∑k=1Knkn​{v⁡(Γ^pl,(k))+ℙn,k​ϕ​(⋅,η^k,ξ^(k))+ℚT,k​ϕT​(⋅,η^k,ξ^(k),v⁡(Γ^pl,(k)))},\widehat{v}^{\textsc{os}}_{-}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{n_{k}}{n}\Bigl\{v\bigl(\widehat{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{pl},(k)}\bigr)+\mathbb{P}_{n,k}\,\phi\bigl(\cdot\,;\widehat{\eta}_{k},\widehat{\xi}^{(k)}\bigr)+\mathbb{Q}_{T,k}\,\phi_{T}\bigl(\cdot\,;\widehat{\eta}_{k},\widehat{\xi}^{(k)},v(\widehat{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{pl},(k)})\bigr)\Bigr\}, (D.5)

with an analogous expression for the upper endpoint.

For our estimator (Algorithm 1), the theory requires small products of nuisance errors and consistency of the optimizer and dual estimates used for the standard error. For the standard one-step correction (Algorithm 2), those estimates also enter the point correction, so theory will require stronger rates on the fitted inputs. It can then be shown that the standard one-step correction is asymptotically equivalent to our estimator and converges to the same limit.

Each replication computes the direct plug-in, our estimator (Algorithm 1), and the standard one-step correction (Algorithm 2) on the same data and outer folds. The sample-size grids are

𝒩linear\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{linear}} ={1,000,2,500,5,000,10,000,20,000,50,000},R=300,\displaystyle=\{1{,}000,2{,}500,5{,}000,10{,}000,20{,}000,50{,}000\},\qquad R=300,
𝒩boosted\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{boosted}} ={500,1,000,2,500,5,000,10,000},R=100.\displaystyle=\{500,1{,}000,2{,}500,5{,}000,10{,}000\},\qquad R=100.

Saturated linear regressions are fit by minimum-norm least squares, and all 4,600 matched replications completed. Per-replication records include the endpoints, standard errors, active branches, branch gaps, span diagnostics, eigenvalues, and solver status.

D.4 Conditional coverage and sign mismatch

Figure 2 in the main text reports sign mismatch probability and average pointwise coverage for the partially identified boosted design. Coverage for the standard one-step correction is conditional on no sign mismatch for either partial identification bound.

The standard one-step correction had no numerical or fold-level feasibility failures. Every declared failure was a sign mismatch across folds. In the partial-linear design, its lower and upper endpoint failure rates were 18.7 and 5.0 percent at n=1,000n=1{,}000, falling to 1.0 and 0 percent at n=2,500n=2{,}500 and to zero thereafter. In the partial-boost design, the rates were 78 and 45 percent at n=500n=500, 28 and 19 percent at n=1,000n=1{,}000, 9 and 2 percent at n=2,500n=2{,}500, and zero from n=5,000n=5{,}000. Our estimator permitted inference in every replication.

D.5 Variance matching and difference between the corrections

At the larger sample sizes, the mean standard errors are close to the Monte Carlo standard deviations for both algorithms. The main mismatches occur for the standard one-step correction in the smallest partial designs, where the reported results are conditional on no sign mismatch for the corresponding partial identification bound.

The standard one-step correction corrects values computed at foldwise fitted inputs, whereas our estimator evaluates the partial identification bound after it pools corrected inputs. Figure 6 compares their absolute endpoint difference with our estimator’s standard error. The scaled difference falls overall as sample size grows, especially with linear nuisance fits. At the largest sample size it is 0.099 of a standard error in the point-linear design and 0.123 and 0.081 for the two partial-linear endpoints. The corresponding ratios are 0.457 in the point-boost design and 0.495 and 0.507 in the partial-boost design. The linear experiments already have small gaps on this scale, while the boosted experiments remain visibly different on this sample grid.

D.6 Practical implementation and sensitivity checks

In addition to the robustness checks reccomended in Section 6.3, we give additional best practices for implementation here. Restrictions should be chosen before the target outcomes are inspected and applied as a sequence of sensitivity checks. First fix the context basis and scaling, which determine what a coefficient restriction means. State the substantive reason for each restriction and add restrictions one at a time so readers can see what changes the partial identification bounds. When a restriction depends on a value such as MM or κ\kappa, report results over a reasonable range. If the restriction sets are nested, the partial identification bounds should also be nested. A failure of nesting indicates an implementation error. Vary one ingredient at a time, including the target profile and the set of source sites. An infeasible result means that the restriction conflicts with the estimated source moments within the chosen model. An unbounded result means that the restriction leaves a direction that affects the target uncontrolled.

Some restrictions, including effect hierarchy, are finite unions of branches. Solve every branch separately and retain its interval. Report the overall endpoints together with these intervals so that any gaps in the identified set remain visible. For each endpoint, report the selected branch and its estimated gap from the closest competing branch. This gap is a useful diagnostic, but it does not prove that the population branch is separated. A small gap or a tie means that branch selection may be unstable and the usual normal approximation may fail. Lemma 3 gives the formal result when the population gap is positive. The standard one-step correction also requires every fold program to be feasible and every fold to select the same branch for a given endpoint. If the folds disagree, report a failed endpoint rather than combining corrections from different branches.

Numerical checks are needed because the optimizer and reduced equality dual enter the influence function. The program should be solved in the reduced site span so that redundant rows of the full equality system do not create artificial dual nonuniqueness. For every endpoint, check primal and dual feasibility. Then check stationarity and complementarity, and confirm that the objective gap is within tolerance. Report the numerical rank within 𝒱C\mathcal{V}_{C}, the smallest reduced eigenvalue, and the dual uniqueness check. The error in the reported value should be negligible relative to n−1/2n^{-1/2}. For our estimator, the optimizer and dual affect the standard error but not the point estimate. For the standard one-step correction, they also enter the point correction, so the accuracy requirements are tighter. Do not replace an infeasible or unbounded result with a clipped finite value. Record the status and include it in the sensitivity analysis.

D.7 Multipliers, branch stability, and reporting

Multiplier structure.

The inequality multiplier ν⋆\nu^{\star} does not enter (B.15), because (G,h)(G,h) is fixed along moment perturbations. The proof in Section B.2 accounts for the changing equality constraints when differentiating the value. The inequality multiplier still determines the equality dual through stationarity (B.18) and hence affects the influence function through λ¯⋆\bar{\lambda}^{\star}.

Branch stability and transfer.

Lemma 3 covers both the local constancy of the selected branch and the op(n−1/2)o_{p}(n^{-1/2}) transfer from the mixed-integer program to the selected convex branch, so no separate selection or transfer lemma is needed. For effect hierarchy, Assumption E requires the unique winning encoding and positive gap described in Section C.2.

Reporting.

Report the estimated branch gap and the dual-uniqueness check as solver diagnostics, and state explicitly that conditioning inference on a reported gap is a pretest rather than a certificate of regularity. Report a path over κ\kappa rather than treating effect hierarchy as a maintained scientific assumption.

Two further checks catch many remaining errors in the partial identification bound calculation. The rank report and the handling of infeasible and unbounded results are already covered in Section D.6.

  1. 1.

    Check ‖ΣC^​β^a−da^‖\|\widehat{\Sigma_{C}}\widehat{\beta}_{a}-\widehat{d_{a}}\| against the solver tolerance for every reported branch.

  2. 2.

    For nested values of κ\kappa, verify that the reported outer intervals are nested in the direction implied by the restriction sets.

D.8 Target sampling and experimental designs

The expansion in (5.4) treats the source and target covariate samples as independent. If QTQ_{T} is known from a census or another effectively deterministic population file, its influence term is omitted. A finite target survey contributes the second term in (5.4). Treating such a survey as fixed without a separate conditional-inference argument understates uncertainty.

Site-specific individual randomization is allowed through ea​(X,C)e_{a}(X,C), and the simulations exercise site-varying probabilities. If treatment is randomized at some within-site cluster (e.g., by village), UaU_{a} must use the cluster design probability and variance estimation must aggregate the influence-function values at the independent randomization unit. The individual-i.i.d. theorem does not justify a cluster-robust application by itself; the application’s standard errors sum influence values within each country’s randomization unit as a design-based correction, and a formal clustered version of Theorem 1 is left to future work.
